parole.significato: Forms nouns (and occasionally adjectives) relating to organisms that inhabit a particular habitat.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French -cole, from Latin -cola (“cultivator”).

parole.significato: digits
parole.testo: From French -dactyle, from Latin -dactylus, ultimately from Ancient Greek δάκτυλος (dáktulos, “finger”).

parole.significato: Diminutive suffix in words of French origin.
parole.testo: Variant of French -eille, from Middle French -eille, from Old French -eille, -eil, -ele, -eyle, from Latin -icula, from rebracketing of -i- + -culus.

parole.significato: The act of creating something, or (more broadly) any process involving the specified thing.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French -faction, from Latin -factiō. This is the ending that arises when forming action nouns using -tiō (equivalent to English -tion) from compound verbs ending in -faciō (“to make, to do”), which carry a causative meaning. parole.significato: Forming nouns denoting the quality or condition of being what is indicated by the first element of the word.
parole.testo: From French -ieté or its source, Latin -ietas.

parole.significato: Suffix denoting ordinal number.
parole.testo: From French -ime, from decime, ultimately from Latin -ima.

parole.significato: Used to form nouns denoting followers or adherents of a specified person, idea, doctrine, movement, etc.
parole.testo: From French -ite, from Old French, from Latin -ītēs, from Ancient Greek -ῑ́της (-ī́tēs).

parole.significato: A branch of learning; a study of a particular subject.
parole.testo: The English -logy suffix originates with loanwords from the Greek, usually via Latin and French, where the suffix -λογία (-logía) is an integral part of the word loaned. parole.significato: Forming adjectives corresponding to nouns in -meter.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French -métrique, from Latin metricus.

parole.significato: Having disease or abnormal condition.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French -otique, from Latin -ōticus, from Ancient Greek -ωτικός (-ōtikós), from -όω (-óō)-stem verbs + -τικός (-tikós). Equivalent to -όω (-óō) + -σις (-sis) + -ικός (-ikós).

parole.significato: Suffix indicating an organism or person with a specified number or type of feet.
parole.testo: Partly from French ‑pède and partly from Latin pedis (genitive of pēs (“foot”)).

parole.significato: Used to form a name of an inhabited place, a town or city.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French ville (“town, city”).

parole.significato: Synonym of nomogram.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from French abaque, from Classical Latin abacus, from Ancient Greek ἄβαξ (ábax). Doublet of abacus and abaque.

parole.significato: A nomogram.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French abaque. Doublet of abacus and abac.

parole.significato: Louvres or strips of wood or metal used as windbreaks that allow light and air in, often seen in belfries.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French abat-vent, from abattre (“to throw down”) + vent (“wind”), from Latin ventus.

parole.significato: A low-ranking member of the Roman Catholic clergy in France who is not a member of a religious order, is not a priest,…
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French abbé (“abbot”), from Latin abbās (“abbot”). Doublet of abbot.

parole.significato: Acting to diminish irritation; soothing.
parole.testo: From ab- (prefix from Latin ab (“from”)) + irritant, from French irritant, from Latin irrītō (“to irritate”).

parole.significato: To send abroad.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French ablégate, from Latin ablēgātus, perfect passive participle of ablēgō (“to send off or away; banish”), from ab (“from, away from”) + lēgō (“to dispatch, send on a commission”). See legate.

parole.significato: Cleansing, detergent.
parole.testo: From French, from Latin abstergens, present participle of abstergeo (“wiping off”).

parole.significato: Prone to treat someone badly by coarse, insulting words or other maltreatment; vituperative; reproachful; scurrilous.
parole.testo: First attested in the 1530s. From French abusif, from Latin abūsīvus, from abusus + -ivus (“-ive”). Equivalent to abuse + -ive.

parole.significato: Lodging in a dwelling or similar living quarters afforded to travellers in hotels or on cruise ships, or students, etc.
parole.testo: From French accommodation, from Latin accommodātiō (“adjustment, accommodation, compliance”), from accommodō (“adapt, put in order”). Superficially accommodate + -ion. The sense of "lodging" was first attested in 1600.

parole.significato: Delivery in childbed; parturition
parole.testo: Borrowed from French accouchement, from French accoucher (“to be delivered of a child, to aid in delivery”), from Old French acouchier (“to lay down, put to bed, go to bed”), from Latin ad- + collocare (“to lay, put, place”). See collate.

parole.significato: A person, especially a man, who delivers a baby (in childbirth).
parole.testo: Attested since 1727. Borrowed from French accoucheur, from accoucher (“to go to childbed, be delivered”), from Old French culcher (“to lie”), from Latin collocō (“to place, put, set in order, assign”), from con- + locō (“to put, place, set”). See accouchement.

parole.significato: A male accuser.
parole.testo: From literary French accusateur, from Latin accūsātōrem, accusative singular of accūsātor (“accuser”). Doublet of accuser.

parole.significato: Sourness of taste, with bitterness and astringency, like that of unripe fruit.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French acerbité, from Latin acerbitās (“acerbity; harshness”), from acerbus (“bitter”). See acerb.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or producing vinegar.
parole.testo: From French acétique, from Latin acētum (“vinegar”), from acēre (“to be sour”). By surface analysis, acet- + -ic.

parole.significato: Sour, sharp, or biting to the taste; tart; having the taste of vinegar.
parole.testo: From French acide, from Latin acidus (“sour, acid”), from aceō (“to be sour”). Doublet of agita.

parole.significato: The quality or state of being acid.
parole.testo: From French acidité, from Latin aciditātem, accusative singular of aciditās (“sourness, acidity”), from acidus (“sour, acid”). Equivalent to acid + -ity.

parole.significato: The herb wolfsbane, or monkshood; any plant of the genus Aconitum, all the species of which are poisonous.
parole.testo: From French aconit, from Latin aconītum, from Ancient Greek ἀκόνιτον (akóniton).

parole.significato: An acroterium.
parole.testo: From French acrotère, from Latin acrōtērium, from Ancient Greek ἀκρωτήριον (akrōtḗrion), from ἄκρος (ákros) + -τήριον (-tḗrion). Doublet of acroterium.

parole.significato: Present, current, living, active.
parole.testo: From French actuel, from Latin actuālis.

parole.significato: The branch of palynology concerned with the study of modern-day pollens and spores, rather than with fossils.
parole.testo: From actuo- (“present, current, living, active”) + palynology, from French actuel, from Latin actuālis + Ancient Greek παλύνω (palúnō, “to sprinkle, scatter”) (from πάλη (pálē, “fine meal, dust”)) + Ancient Greek -λογία (-logía). By surface analysis, actuo- + palyno- + -log + -y.

parole.significato: Well skilled; completely versed; thoroughly proficient.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French adepte, from Latin adeptus (“who has achieved”), the past participle of adipisci (“to attain”).

parole.significato: The ability of a substance to stick to an unlike substance.
parole.testo: From French adhésion, from Latin stem of adhaesio, from past participle of adhaerare.

parole.significato: The act of adopting.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French adoption, from Latin adoptio, allied to adoptare (“to adopt”). Equivalent to adopt + -ion.

parole.significato: Synonym of adorer.
parole.testo: From French adorateur and its etymon Latin adōrātor. By surface analysis, adore + -ator or adorate + -or.

parole.significato: deft, dexterous, or skillful
parole.testo: Borrowed from French adroit, from French à (“on the; to”) (from Old French a (“to; towards”), from Latin ad (“to; towards”), from Proto-Indo-European *ád (“at; near”)) + French droit (“right”) (from Old French droit, dreit, from Late Latin drictus, syncopated form of Latin dīrēctus (“laid straight;

parole.significato: To accumulate on a surface, by adsorption.
parole.testo: From French adsorber, from Latin ad- (“to”) + sorbeō (“suck in”).

parole.significato: Flattery; fulsome praise.
parole.testo: From French adulation, from Latin adulātio (“flattery”).

parole.significato: An animal that is full-grown.
parole.testo: From French adulte, from Latin adultus (“grown up”), perfect passive participle of adolescō (“to grow up”). Compare adolescent.

parole.significato: A word that modifies a verb, adjective, other adverbs, or various other types of words, phrases, or clauses.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French adverbe, from Latin adverbium, from ad- (“to”) + verb(um) (“word, verb”) + -ium, so called because it is used to supplement other words (not specifically verbs). By surface analysis, ad- + verb.

parole.significato: A steam engine powered by rocket propulsion due to escaping steam, consisting of a pressure vessel mounted on a bearing…
parole.testo: From French éolipyle, from Latin Aeoli pylae (“doorway of Aeolus”).

parole.significato: Of or belonging to the atmosphere or to the air; aerial.
parole.testo: From the French aérien, from the Old French aerïen, from the Classical Latin āerius; compare aerial.

parole.significato: Receiving others kindly and conversing with them in a free and friendly manner; friendly, courteous, sociable.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French affable, from Latin affābilis, from affor (“to address”), from ad + for (“to speak, to talk”). See fable. By surface analysis, af- + fable.

parole.significato: To cause (somebody) to die of hunger; to starve.
parole.testo: From French affamer, from Latin ad + fames (“hunger”). Compare famish.

parole.significato: The brain’s reception of signals from the body.
parole.testo: Adjective form of afferent, from French afférent (“which brings inward”), from Latin afferent-, from afferēns, present participle of afferre (“bring to”), from af- (variant of ad-) + ferre (“bear”). Doublet of afferentia.

parole.significato: The relationship resulting from affiliating one thing with another.
parole.testo: From French affiliation, from Latin affiliatiō, noun of action from verb affiliō, from af- (form of ad- (“to”) before an f) + filiō (from filius (“son”)).

parole.significato: The act of agitating, or the state of being agitated; the state of being disrupted with violence, or with irregular act…
parole.testo: From French agitation, from Latin agitātiō (“movement, agitation”).

parole.significato: of the male bloodline; patrilineal
parole.testo: From French agnatique, from Latin agnātus (“paternal kinsman”). Equivalent to agnate + -ic.

parole.significato: A tube through which is water is discharged; an efflux tube.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French ajutage, from ajoutage, from ajouter (“to add”), from Latin adjuxtare, from ad + juxta (“near to, nigh”). Compare adjutage, adjustage, adjust.

parole.significato: The state of being winged.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French, from Latin alatus (“winged”).

parole.significato: Any of a class of monomeric proteins that are soluble in water, and are coagulated by heat; they occur in egg white, mi…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French albumine, from Latin albumen. Compare albumen.

parole.significato: Food.
parole.testo: From French aliment, from Latin alimentum (“food”).

parole.significato: Contained in the whole an integral number of times, a factor or divisor.
parole.testo: From French aliquote, from Latin aliquot.

parole.significato: Any of certain shad:
parole.testo: Borrowed from French alose, from Latin alausa, from unattested Gaulish *alausa. Cognate with German Alse.

parole.significato: A very high mountain. Specifically, one of the Alps, the highest chain of mountains in Europe.
parole.testo: Late Middle English, back-formation from alps pl, via French from Latin Alpes (“high mountains, especially those of Switzerland”). Compare Old Saxon elbon (“Alps”), Old High German Alpūn (“Alps”); Old High German alba (“alp, mountain”)).

parole.significato: Of or relating to an alphabet, especially the characters A to Z, both uppercase and lowercase.
parole.testo: Partly from French alphabétique and partly from its etymon Latin alphabēticus. By surface analysis, alphabet + -ic.

parole.significato: A lover, especially if illicit; a paramour.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French amant, from Latin amantem, present participle of amō.

parole.significato: A lover of something.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French amateur, from Latin amātor (“lover”), from amāre (“to love”).

parole.significato: Evasive or ambiguous language; circumlocution.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English ambages, from French ambage as well as its etymon Latin ambāgēs (“a roundabout or circuitous path”).

parole.significato: Starch modified by heat so as to become a transparent mass, like horn. It is soluble in cold water.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French amidine, from amido (“starch”), from Latin amylum.

parole.significato: That lives by a river.
parole.testo: From French amnicole, from Latin amnicola + -ous.

parole.significato: Amphiboly.
parole.testo: From French amphibologie, from late Latin amphibologia, earlier amphibolia, from Ancient Greek ἀμφιβολία (amphibolía, “ambiguity”).

parole.significato: To amputate (a limb).
parole.testo: Borrowed from French amputer (“to amputate”) or its etymon Latin amputāre, amputō. Doublet of amputate, which was borrowed through the past participle amputātus.

parole.significato: A person who has had one or more limbs removed.
parole.testo: From French amputée, (past participle of amputer (“to amputate”)), from Latin amputatus, perfect passive participle of amputare (“to amputate”).

parole.significato: A spiced, heavily smoked Cajun pork sausage, often made from the entire gastrointestinal system of the pig.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French andouille, ultimately from Latin indūcō (“to lead in, to bring in”). Doublet of nduja.

parole.significato: A person who is androgynous.
parole.testo: From French androgyne, from Latin androgynus.

parole.significato: Breathing difficulty, shortness of breath.
parole.testo: From French anhélation, or directly from its etymon Latin anhēlātiō (“shortness of breath, gasping, panting, puffing”) (compare Late Latin anhēlātiō (“desire; eager pursuit”)), from anhēlātus (“exhaled”) + -iō (suffix forming abstract nouns from verbs). Anhēlātus is the perfect passive participle of

parole.significato: Violent hatred leading to active opposition; active enmity; energetic dislike.
parole.testo: From French animosité, from Latin animositas (“courage, spirit, vehemence”), from animosus, from animus (“courage, spirit, mind”); see animose, animate.

parole.significato: An addition, an extension.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French annexe, from Latin annexus. More at Etymology 2. See also an-.

parole.significato: Having existed in ancient times, descended from antiquity; used especially in reference to Greece and Rome.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French antique (“ancient, old”), from Latin antiquus (“former, earlier, ancient, old”), from ante (“before”); see ante-. Doublet of antic.

parole.significato: A vassal or bodyguard of Merovingian kings.
parole.testo: From French, from Latin antrustio; compare Latin trustis.

parole.significato: A grant (especially by a sovereign) of land (or other source of revenue) as a birthright.
parole.testo: From French apanage, from Latin *appanare, adpanare (“to give bread”), from pānis (“bread”).

parole.significato: Lack of emotion or motivation; lack of interest or enthusiasm towards something; disinterest (in something).
parole.testo: From French apathie, from Latin apathīa, from Ancient Greek ἀπάθεια (apátheia, “impassibility”, “insensibility”, “freedom from emotion”), from ἀπαθής (apathḗs, “not suffering or having suffered”, “without experience of”), from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + πάθος (páthos, “anything that befalls one”, “incident”,

parole.significato: Having the character of apology; regretfully excusing.
parole.testo: From French apologétique, from Latin apologēticus, from Ancient Greek ἀπολογητικός (apologētikós, “of or suitable for defense”), from ἀπολογέομαι (apologéomai, “to speak in defense of”); see more at English apology.

parole.significato: A short story with a moral, often involving talking animals or objects; a fable.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French apologue, from Latin apologus from Ancient Greek ἀπόλογος (apólogos, “story, tale, fable”) from ἀπό- (apó-, “off, away from”) + λόγος (lógos, “speech”). Equivalent to apo- + -logue.

parole.significato: A marginal note; a gloss.
parole.testo: From French postille (“marginal note”), from Latin post illa (verba) (“after those (words)”).

parole.significato: A special certification established in 1961 for certifying foreign documents.
parole.testo: From French apostille (“a marginal note”), from Latin post (“after”) + illa (“these”) + verba (“words”).

parole.significato: The text character ’, which serves as a punctuation mark in various languages and as a diacritical mark in certain rare…
parole.testo: From French apostrophe, or Latin apostrophus, from Ancient Greek ἀπόστροφος (apóstrophos, “accent of elision”), a noun use of an adjective from ἀποστρέφω (apostréphō, “to turn away”), from ἀπό (apó, “away from”) + στρέφω (stréphō, “to turn”).

parole.significato: The state or action of desiring or craving.
parole.testo: Circa 1600, from French appétence, from Latin appetentia, from appetere (“to seek after”). Doublet of appetite.

parole.significato: To make (someone or oneself) aware of some information; to inform, to notify.
parole.testo: PIE word  *h₂éd Borrowed from French appris, apprise, the past participle form of apprendre (“to learn; to teach”), from Middle French apprendre, aprendre (“to learn”), from Old French aprendre, aprandre (“to learn; to educate, teach”), from Latin apprēndere, a variant of apprehendere, adprehendere,

parole.significato: To prop or support, e.g. by posting troops.
parole.testo: From French appui, from Latin ad + podium (“foothold”).

parole.significato: The study of the spider, a branch of arachnology.
parole.testo: From French aranéologie, from Latin arānea + French -o- + -logie. By surface analysis, araneo- + -logy.

parole.significato: Relating to arbitration.
parole.testo: From French arbitral, from Latin arbitrālis, from arbiter.

parole.significato: An axis or shaft supporting a rotating part on a lathe.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French arbre (“tree, axis”), spelling influenced by Latin arbor (“tree”).

parole.significato: An antiquarian; an archaeologist.
parole.testo: From French archéologue, from post-classical Latin archaiologus or its etymon Byzantine Greek ἀρχαιολόγος (arkhaiológos), from Ancient Greek ἀρχαιο- (arkhaio-) + -λογος (-logos). Equivalent to archaeo- + -logue.

parole.significato: The territory (principality) of an archduke.
parole.testo: From French archiduché, from Middle French, itself from archi- (“arch-”) < Latin archi- + duché (“duchy, dukedom”) < Latin dux (“leader, commander, duke”).

parole.significato: The chief, or highest-ranked physician of a prince, city or country, such as the Holy Roman Empire
parole.testo: From French archiâtre, from Latin archīāter. Compare arch-, iatro-, -iatry.

parole.significato: The superior of a large monastery, or group of monasteries, in the Orthodox Church.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French archimandrite, from Latin archimandrīta, from late Ancient Greek ἀρχιμανδρίτης (arkhimandrítēs), from ἀρχι- (arkhi-, “highest”) + μάνδρα (mándra, “enclosure, cloister, monastery”) + -ῑ́της (-ī́tēs, “member of”).

parole.significato: The art and science of designing and managing the construction of buildings and other structures, particularly if they…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French architecture, from Latin architectūra. Originally from architect, from Ancient Greek ἀρχιτέκτων (arkhitéktōn, “architect”, literally “arch builder, ext. chief builder, principal craftsman”).

parole.significato: Chiefly in the form archives.
parole.testo: The noun is borrowed from French archive, archif, from Late Latin archīvum, archīum (“archive; room containing an archive; public record office”), from Ancient Greek ἀρχεῖον (arkheîon, “office of a magistrate; public building or office; town hall; (in the plural) archives; public records”), a noun u

parole.significato: Any of the smallest enclosures created by the veins of a leaf.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French aréole, from Latin areola: a small area. Doublet of areola.

parole.significato: Silver material, or silverness in color.
parole.testo: From French argenterie, from argent (“silver”), from Latin argentum.

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or using arithmetic; arithmetical.
parole.testo: From French arithmétique, from Latin arithmēticus, from Ancient Greek ἀριθμητῐκός (arithmētĭkós).

parole.significato: A fabric woven with a raised pattern similar to chain mail.
parole.testo: From French armure, from Middle French armure, from Old French armeure, from Latin armātūra. Doublet of armature and armor.

parole.significato: The act of arresting.
parole.testo: From French arrestation, from Latin arrestatio.

parole.significato: One of the small branches of an artery, especially one that connects with capillaries.
parole.testo: From French artériole, from Latin arteriola, from Latin artēria.

parole.significato: A very thin ridge of rock.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French arête, from Latin arista. Doublet of arista.

parole.significato: she-ass.
parole.testo: French asine, from Latin asina.

parole.significato: A nonessential amino acid C₄H₈N₂O₃ found in plants such as asparagus.
parole.testo: From French asparagine, from Latin asparagus + French -ine. By surface analysis, asparagus + -ine.

parole.significato: A meat or fish jelly.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French aspic, from Latin aspis, and possibly influenced by French basilic (“basilisk”). parole.significato: Someone who aspires (for high office, etc.)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French aspirant.

parole.significato: Roasting, baking.
parole.testo: From French assation, from Latin assare (“to roast”).

parole.significato: acquisition; an obtaining
parole.testo: From French assécution, from Latin assequi (“to obtain”), from ad + sequi (“to follow”).

parole.significato: The repetition of similar or identical vowel sounds (though with different consonants), usually in literature or poetry.
parole.testo: From French assonance, from Latin assonāre; by surface analysis, a- + son- + -ance.

parole.significato: A reduction in the functionality of an organ caused by disease, injury or lack of use.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French atrophie, from Latin atrophia, from Ancient Greek ἀτροφία (atrophía, “a wasting away”), from ἄτροφος (átrophos, “ill-fed, un-nourished”), from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + τροφή (trophḗ, “nourishment”), from τρέφω (tréphō, “to fatten”). Equivalent to a- + -trophy.

parole.significato: The space, often unfinished and with sloped walls, directly below the roof in the uppermost part of a house or other bu…
parole.testo: From the practice of decorating the top storey of building facades in the Attic architectural style. From French attique, from Latin atticus, from Ancient Greek Ἀττικός (Attikós).

parole.significato: In a natural state; without any artificial change; natural; also, done in a way to appear natural.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French au naturel (“in the natural state; cooked plainly”), from au (“at the; in the; to the”) + naturel (“natural”) (ultimately borrowed from Latin nātūrālis (“of or relating to nature”), from nātūra (“natural world, nature”) + -ālis (suffix forming adjectives of relationsh

parole.significato: A priming tube connecting the charge chamber with the gallery, or place where the slow match is applied.
parole.testo: From French, diminutive of auge (“trough”), from Latin alveus (“hollow”), from alvus (“belly”).

parole.significato: Awe-inspiring, majestic, noble, venerable.
parole.testo: From French auguste (“noble, stately; august”) or Latin augustus (“majestic, venerable, august; imperial, royal”), from augeō (“to augment, increase; to enlarge, expand, spread”). Doublet of August and Augustus.

parole.significato: A strong, pressurized, heated vessel, as for laboratory experiments, sterilization, cooking or mineral processing.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French autoclave, formed with prefix auto- + Latin clavis (“key”).

parole.significato: A broad street, especially one bordered by trees or, in cities laid out in a grid pattern, one that is on a particular…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French avenue, from Old French avenue, feminine past participle of avenir (“approach”), from Latin adveniō, advenīre (“come to”, from ad (“to”) + veniō, venīre (“come”)).

parole.significato: The art or science of making and flying aircraft.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French aviation, derived from Latin avis (“bird”). By surface analysis, avi- + -ation.

parole.significato: Enthusiastic; keen; eager; showing great interest in something or desire to do something.
parole.testo: From French avide, from Latin avidus (“eager, desirous; greedy”), from aveō (“wish, desire, long for, crave”).

parole.significato: The axle of a wheel.
parole.testo: Derived from French axe, from Latin axis.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the axilla or armpit.
parole.testo: Alteration by association with -ary of the French axillaire (“of the axilla”), itself an alteration of the earlier forms aisselliere and aissellaire, both from the assumed Latin etymon *axillāris, from axilla (“armpit”), diminutive form of the assumed *axula.

parole.significato: Fat or grease, especially of a pig or goose.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French axonge (“lard”), from Latin axungia, from axis (“wheel”) + ungere (“to grease, lubricate”).

parole.significato: A counterbalanced structure having one end that rises as the other lowers.
parole.testo: From French bascule, from earlier French bacule, from Old French bacul, from Old French battre + cul, from Latin battuō (“beat”) + cul (“bottom”).

parole.significato: A baton.
parole.testo: From French bâton, from Latin bastum (“stick”).

parole.significato: A large game or fish pie made with small pieces of offal.
parole.testo: Corrupted from French béatilles, diminutive formed from Latin beatus.

parole.significato: A form of hunting in which game is forced into the open by the beating of sticks on bushes, etc.
parole.testo: From French battue, ultimately from Latin battere. Doublet of battuta, which arrived via Italian.

parole.significato: Relating to, or relieving, a cough.
parole.testo: From French béchique or its source Latin bēchicus (“of or for a cough”), from Ancient Greek βηχικός (bēkhikós, “of or for a cough”), from βηχ- (bēkh-), oblique stem of βήξ (bḗx, “cough”).

parole.significato: An attractive woman.
parole.testo: From French belle (“beautiful”), from Latin bella.

parole.significato: warlike; bellicose
parole.testo: Borrowed from French bellique, itself from Latin bellicus.

parole.significato: A monk or nun belonging to the order founded by Saint Benedict of Nursia.
parole.testo: From French bénédictin, from Latin benedictus, named after Italian 6th century Saint Benedict of Nursia (Latin: Benedictus Nursiae). Recorded in English from the 17th century. By surface analysis, Benedict + -ine.

parole.significato: An exorcist, the third of the four lesser orders in the Roman Catholic church.
parole.testo: From French [Term?], from Latin benedictus (“blessed”).

parole.significato: The vase or vessel for holy water in Roman Catholic churches.
parole.testo: From French bénitier, from Latin benedictarium, benedictus.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Saint Bernard of Clairvaux, or to the Cistercian monks.
parole.testo: From French Bernardin or Latin Bernardīnus. By surface analysis, Bernard + -ine.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to something containing or consisting of bile.
parole.testo: From French bilieux, from Latin bīliōsus (“full of bile”), from bīlis (“bile”) + -ōsus (“full of”).

parole.significato: Synonym of biarchy.
parole.testo: From French binarchie, from Latin bīnī (“twin”) + -archia (“-archy”), from Ancient Greek -αρχία (-arkhía, “-archy: rule”).

parole.significato: A kind of double-barrelled field glass or opera glass.
parole.testo: From French binocle, from Latin bi- (“two”) + oculus (“eye”).

parole.significato: An extremely bright meteor.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French bolide, from Latin bolis, from Ancient Greek βολίς (bolís, “missile, arrow, javelin”). Doublet of bolis.

parole.significato: A clear seasoned broth made by simmering usually light meat, such as beef or chicken.
parole.testo: First attested 1656, from French bouillon, from the verb bouillir (“to boil”), from Old French boillir, from Latin bullīre (“to bubble, boil”), from bulla (“bubble”).

parole.significato: A stock exchange.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French bourse, from Old French borse, from Latin bursa, from Ancient Greek βύρσα (búrsa). Doublet of purse, compare Danish børs, Swedish börs, German Börse. See also bursar.

parole.significato: Braccae, breeches; an undergarment worn in medieval Europe.
parole.testo: From French braies, from Old French braies, plural of braie, from Latin braca.

parole.significato: One of two species of acanthus, Acanthus spinosus or Acanthus mollis; bear's breech.

parole.significato: A native or inhabitant of the region of Brittany, France.
parole.testo: From French Breton. Doublet of Briton and Brython.

parole.significato: Mist, fog, vapour.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French brume, from Latin brūma (“winter solstice; winter; winter cold”). parole.significato: very dry, and not sweet
parole.testo: From French brut (“raw”), from Middle French brut, from Old French brut, from Latin brūtus (“heavy”).

parole.significato: An alkaloid, found in the skins of some toads, related to serotonin.
parole.testo: From French bufoténine, from Latin bufo (“toad”) + ten- (uncertain element) + -ine.

parole.significato: Any of several plants in the borage family, Boraginaceae.

parole.significato: A freshwater fish, taxonomic name Lota lota, which is similar to the ling and the cusk and spawns in the winter.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French barbote, from Latin barba (“a beard”). Displaced native eelpout.

parole.significato: A precious stone which has only been polished, not cut into facets.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French cabochon, diminutive form of caboche (“head”), from Old French caboce, from Latin caput (“head”).

parole.significato: Causing or involving calamity; disastrous.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French calamiteux (“calamitous”) (see French -eux, English -ous), from Latin calamitōsus (“destructive, disastrous, ruinous, calamitous”), a contraction of calamitātōsus, from calamitāt- + -ōsus (suffix meaning ‘full of; prone to’ forming adjectives from nouns); calamitāt- is the obliq

parole.significato: A reckoning; computation.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French calcul, derived from Latin calculus (“reckoning”). Doublet of calculus.

parole.significato: To copy (a drawing) by rubbing the back of it with red or black chalk, and then passing a blunt stylus or needle over t…
parole.testo: From French calque, ultimately derived from Latin calcō (“to trample”). Doublet of calque.

parole.significato: Relating to calories.
parole.testo: From calorie + -ic. From French calorique, coined by French chemist Antoine Lavoisier, from Latin calor (“heat”).

parole.significato: A non-SI unit of energy, equivalent to 4.184 kilojoules, that can raise the temperature of a kilogram of water by one d…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French calorie, formed from Latin calor. It was originally defined as the large calorie in the early 19th century, with the small calorie being defined some decades later.

parole.significato: An apparatus for conveying and distributing heat, especially by means of hot water circulating in tubes.
parole.testo: From French calorifère, from Latin calor (“heat”) + ferre (“to bear”).

parole.significato: Relating to calories.
parole.testo: From French calorifique or Latin calorificus, from calor + -i- + -ficus.

parole.significato: Synonym of dog days.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French canicule, from Latin. Doublet of chenille.

parole.significato: An artillery soldier who maintains and operates (historical) a cannon, or (now) some other piece of heavy artillery.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French canonnier, with the ending reshaped to English -eer (suffix forming agent nouns denoting people associated with, concerned with, or engaged in specified activities). parole.significato: The part of a bit which is put in a horse's mouth.
parole.testo: From French canon, from Latin canon (“a rule”).

parole.significato: A steel skullcap formerly worn by members of the military.
parole.testo: From French capeline, from Latin cappella.

parole.significato: The former chief magistrates of the city of Toulouse, France.
parole.testo: From French capitoul, from the Capitole de Toulouse, the town's city hall (est. 1190). The name referenced the Roman Capitol and the town's Latin capitulum (“charter; chapter”). Doublet of capitol and Capitolium.

parole.testo: From French capsien, from Latin Capsianus, from Capsa (“Gafsa”) + -ianus (“-ian”).

parole.significato: A membranous envelope.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French capsule, from Latin capsula, diminutive of capsa (“box”).

parole.significato: To send a carbon copy of an email message to.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French carbone, coined by Antoine Lavoisier, from Latin carbō, carbōnem (“charcoal, coal”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *kerh₃- (“to burn”).

parole.significato: The lower portion of a marine animal's shell, covering its mantle.
parole.testo: From French carène (“keel”), from Latin carīna (“keel”).

parole.significato: An organism that feeds chiefly on animals; an animal that feeds on meat as the main part of its diet.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French carnivore, from Latin carnivorus. In the zoological sense, coined by William Whewell in 1840 as an adaptation of Cuvier's coinage, French carnivore.

parole.significato: A large European sailing vessel of the 14th to 17th centuries similar to a caravel but square-rigged on the foremast an…
parole.testo: From French caraque (compare Spanish and Portuguese carraca, Italian caracca), from Latin carraca, from Latin carrus (“wagon”); or perhaps from Arabic قَرَاقِير (qarāqīr).

parole.significato: A bill of fare; a menu.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French carte, from Latin charta. Doublet of card and chart.

parole.significato: A usually translucent and somewhat elastic, dense, nonvascular connective tissue found in various forms in the larynx a…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French cartilage, from Latin cartilāgō. Partially displaced native gristle, from Old English gristel.

parole.significato: A protein present in both milk and in the seeds of leguminous plants.
parole.testo: From French caséine, formed from Latin cāseus (“cheese”) + -ine.

parole.significato: The abrogation of a law by a higher authority; annulment.
parole.testo: From French cassation, from Latin cassō (“destroy, annul”).

parole.significato: A blackcurrant plant (Ribes nigrum); the flavor of its berries.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French cassis (“black currant”), probably from Latin cassia, from Hebrew קציעה (qetzi'ah).

parole.significato: A sudden, violent event.
parole.testo: From French cataclysme, from Latin cataclysmus, from Ancient Greek κατακλυσμός (kataklusmós, “deluge, flood”), from κατακλύζω (kataklúzō, “to dash over, flood, deluge, inundate”), from κατά (katá, “downwards, towards”) + κλύζω (klúzō, “to wash off, to wash away, to dash over”).

parole.significato: Waterfall; cataract.
parole.testo: From French catadupe, from Latin Catadūpa, name of the first cataract of the Nile, from Ancient Greek Κατάδουποι (Katádoupoi); see Catadupe for more.

parole.significato: Acting as a cause.
parole.testo: From French causatif, from Latin causātīvus (“causative, pertaining to a lawsuit, accusative”), from causa (“cause”); see cause (verb) and -ive.

parole.significato: A hot iron for searing or cauterizing.
parole.testo: From French cautère, Latin cauterium, from Ancient Greek καυτήρ (kautḗr), variant of καυστήρ (kaustḗr, “cauterizing apparatus”), from καίω (kaíō, “burn”)). Compare caustic, cautery.

parole.significato: A pale green colour, possibly tinted with gray.
parole.testo: Borrowed from the French céladon, from the character named Céladon, who wore pale green ribbons, in the novel L'Astrée by Honoré d'Urfé, from Latin Celadon, a warrior's name in Ovid's Metamorphoses, related to Ancient Greek κέλᾰδος (kélădos, “din, clamour”).

parole.significato: A person who officiates at a religious ceremony, especially a marriage or the Eucharist.
parole.testo: From French célébrant, from Latin celebrāns, present participle of celebrō, equivalent to celebrate + -ant.

parole.significato: Swift, speedy, fast.
parole.testo: From celerity, from French célérité, from Latin celeritas, from celer (“fast, swift”).

parole.significato: A celibate state; celibacy.
parole.testo: From French célibat (“celibacy”), from Latin caelibātus (“celibacy”), from caelebs (“unmarried”); compare German Zölibat (“celibacy”). Equivalent to Latin caelebs + -ate (forming nouns denoting a rank, a state)

parole.significato: salt cellar
parole.testo: From 15th century English saler, from French salière, from Latin salarius (“relating to salt”), from Latin sal (“salt”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Celts.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French celtique or Latin celticus, equivalent to Celt + -ic. First attested in the 17th century.

parole.significato: one-hundredth
parole.testo: From French centi- and its etymon Latin centi-, from centum (“hundred”). Doublet of hecato- and hecto-.

parole.significato: Any arthropod of class Chilopoda, which have a segmented body with one pair of legs per segment and from about 20 to 30…
parole.testo: From French centipède, from Latin centipeda, centipēs, from centi- (“hundred”) + pēs (“foot”); equivalent to centi- + -pede.

parole.significato: A device in which a mixture of denser and lighter materials (normally dispersed in a liquid) is separated by being spun…
parole.testo: From French centrifuge, from Latin centrum (“center”) + fugiō (“to flee”). Equivalent to centri- + -fuge.

parole.significato: A type of grass (such as wheat, rice or oats) cultivated for its edible grains.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French céréale (“having to do with cereal”), from Latin Cerealis (“of or relating to Ceres”), from Ceres (“Roman goddess of agriculture”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱer- (“grow”), from which also Latin sincerus (English sincere) and Latin crēscō (“grow”) (English crescent). parole.significato: Of or relating to the brain, cerebrum, or cerebral cortex.
parole.testo: Borrowing from French cérébral, from Latin cerebrum (“a brain”); equivalent to cerebrum + -al.

parole.significato: Synonym of white lead, a hydrate of lead mixed with carbonate, particularly as used to whiten skin or in early medicine.
parole.testo: From French céruse, from Latin cērusa, variant of cērussa, q.v.

parole.significato: A metal skullcap.
parole.testo: From French cervelière, from Latin.

parole.significato: Culantro (Eryngium foetidum), a tropical herb whose leaves are used medicinally and in Caribbean cuisine.

parole.significato: Copper(II) sulfate (CuSO₄).
parole.testo: Borrowed from French calcante or Latin chalcanthum.

parole.significato: Skin lesion, sometimes associated with certain contagious diseases such as syphilis.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French chancre (“cancer”), from Latin cancer (“crab”). Cognate to canker and cancer.

parole.significato: A branched, often ornate, light fixture suspended from a ceiling.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French chandelier, from Latin candelabrum, from candela (“a candle”). Doublet of candelabrum. See also candle.

parole.significato: Any song with French words, but more specifically a classic, lyric-driven French song.
parole.testo: From French chanson f (“song”), from Latin cantio f. Doublet of cantion and canzone.

parole.significato: A male singer; often specifically a popular or cabaret singer.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French chanteur (“male singer”).

parole.significato: A rectangular steel or iron frame into which pages or columns of type are locked for printing or plate-making.
parole.testo: Perhaps from French châsse (“case”, “reliquary”), from Old French chasse, from Latin capsa. Doublet of case, cash, and chasse.

parole.significato: The base frame of a vehicle, such as a motor vehicle.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French châssis, from châsse, from Latin capsa (“case”).

parole.significato: The chickpea.
parole.testo: From French chiche, pois chiche (“a dwarf pea”), from Latin cicer (“the chickpea”).

parole.testo: Calque of French pois chiche, from pois (“pea”) + chiche, from Old French cice, from Latin cicer (“chickpea”).

parole.testo: From French chitine, from Latin chitōn (“mollusk”), from Ancient Greek χιτών (khitṓn). See also chiton.

parole.significato: Related to chitin.
parole.testo: From the noun chitin, from French chitine, from Latin chitōn (“mollusk”), from Ancient Greek χιτών (khitṓn).

parole.significato: An abnormal downward curve to the erect penis.
parole.testo: From French (chaude-pisse) cordée (“corded (urethral discharge)”), ultimately from Latin chorda, from Ancient Greek χορδή (khordḗ, “entrails, intestines”).

parole.testo: Borrowed from French chromatique (“chromatic”) or directly from its etymon Latin chrōmaticus, from Ancient Greek χρωματικός (khrōmatikós, “relating to colour; one of the three types of tetrachord in Greek music”), from χρῶμα (khrôma, “colour; pigment; chromatic scale in music; music”) (ultimately fr

parole.significato: A chronicle.
parole.testo: From French, from Latin, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: A French castle, fortress, manor house, or large country house.
parole.testo: Originated 1730–40. Unadapted borrowing from French château, from Old French chastel, from Latin castellum. Doublet of cashel, castell, castellum, and castle.

parole.significato: A garment or undergarment made of coarse cloth or animal hair worn close to the skin used by members of various Christi…
parole.testo: From French cilice, from Latin cilicium (“clothing made of goatskin”), from Cilicia where it originates from.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a circulation, especially to the circulatory system.
parole.testo: From French circulatoire, from Latin circulatorius.

parole.significato: A Roman circus.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French cirque (“circular arena; cirque”), from Latin circus (“circle, ring”), from Ancient Greek κίρκος (kírkos, “circle, ring; racecourse, circus”), possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to bend; to turn”). Doublet of circus.

parole.significato: A member of a monastic order which follows the Benedictine rule and emphasizes silent contemplative prayer.
parole.testo: From French cistercien, from Latin Cistercium (“Cîteaux”), after the place where the order was founded.

parole.significato: A small citrus tree, Citrus medica.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French citron (“lemon, lime”), Latin citrus (“citron tree, thuja”), probably via Etruscan derived from Ancient Greek κέδρος (kédros, “cedar”) (see there for further etymology).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to citronellic acid.
parole.testo: From French citronelle, ultimately from Latin citron, a type of lemon tree; with suffix -ic.

parole.significato: Having, pertaining to, or involving clairaudience.
parole.testo: Modelled on clairvoyant; from French clair (“clear”) + English audient, or, Latin audient(em) (“hearing”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the first class or rank, especially in literature or art.
parole.testo: From French classique, from Latin classic(us) (“relating to the classes of Roman citizenry, especially the highest”), from classis. By surface analysis, class + -ic. Piecewise doublet of classy.

parole.significato: The keyboard of an organ, pianoforte, or harmonium.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French clavier (“keyboard”), from Latin clavis (“key”).

parole.significato: The body or class of people who frequent an establishment or purchase a service, especially when considered as forming…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French clientèle, ultimately from Latin cliēns (English client).

parole.significato: Having little difference or distance in place, position, or abstractly; see also close to.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French clos, from Latin clausum, participle of claudō.

parole.significato: Reasonable and convincing; based on evidence.
parole.testo: From French cogent, from Latin cōgēns, present active participle of cōgō (“drive together, compel”), from cō + agō (“drive”).

parole.significato: State of cohering, or of working together.
parole.testo: Attested from the late 17th century, borrowed from French cohésion, from Latin cohaesiō, cohaesiōnem.

parole.significato: A dip on a mountain ridge between two peaks.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French col, from Latin collum (“neck”). Doublet of collum.

parole.significato: To coax (someone); also, to flatter (someone).
parole.testo: First attested in 1590s (as colloguing), presumably from colleague (“to associate”) and French colloque (“secret meeting”), from Latin colloquium (English colloquy), possibly influenced by dialogue. parole.significato: The act or art of coloring.
parole.testo: From French coloration, from Latin colōrātiō.

parole.significato: A peddler of publications, especially of religious books
parole.testo: Borrowed from French colporteur, from comporteur by influence of col (“neck”) (re-analyzed as col + porteur (“porter”)), from verb comporter, from Latin comportō (English comport).

parole.significato: An entertainer who performs in a humorous manner, especially by telling jokes.
parole.testo: From French comédien, from comédie + -ien, from Old French comedie, from Latin cōmoedia, from Ancient Greek κωμῳδία (kōmōidía). By surface analysis, comed(y) + -ian.

parole.significato: A confection, especially of preserved fruit.
parole.testo: From French confiture, from Latin confectūra.

parole.significato: A commanding officer, usually of a specific force or division.
parole.testo: From French commandant.

parole.significato: One entrusted with a (small) commission, such as an errand; especially, an attendant or subordinate employee in a publi…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French commissionaire, from Latin commissio. Doublet of commissioner.

parole.significato: Substitution of one thing for another; interchange.
parole.testo: From French commutation, from Latin commūtātiōnem, accusative singular of commūtātiō.

parole.significato: Somebody from one's own country.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French compatriote, itself borrowed from Latin compatriota. By surface analysis, com- + patriot. Displaced native Old English ġelanda.

parole.significato: Compliant.
parole.testo: From French complaisant (“willing to please”), from complaire, from Latin complacēre (“please well”), from com- (“with”) + placeō (“please”).

parole.significato: Made up of multiple parts; composite; not simple.
parole.testo: From French complexe, from Latin complexus, past participle of complector (“to entwine, encircle, compass, infold”), from com- (“together”) and plectō (“to weave, braid”). May be analyzed as com- + -plex. See complect. Doublet of complexus.

parole.significato: Divided into a line of squares of alternating tinctures.
parole.testo: From French componé, from Old French compondre, from Latin compōnere (“put together, arrange, compile”). Cognate with English compose, compound.

parole.significato: A person who sets type; a typesetter.
parole.testo: From French compositeur, from Latin compositor.

parole.significato: Uncontrolled or reactive and irresistible.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French compulsif, formed from Latin compulsus, past participle of compellere (“to compel”), from com- (“together”) + pellere (“to drive”).

parole.significato: To reckon, calculate.
parole.testo: 17th century. Borrowed from French computer, from Latin computō (“calculate, compute”). Doublet of count.

parole.significato: Pertaining to a count.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French comtal, from oblique stem of Latin comes, comitis (“count, earl, companion, comrade”) + -al. Doublet of comital.

parole.significato: Synonym of concher (“machine used to refine the flavour and texture of chocolate”).
parole.testo: Borrowed from French conche.

parole.significato: Synonym of conciseness (“brevity or terseness”).
parole.testo: Borrowed from French concision, from Latin concisiō(n).

parole.significato: occurrence or existence together or in connection with one another, coexistence
parole.testo: First attested in 1607, from French concomitant, from Latin concomitari (“accompany”), from con- (“together”) + comitari (“to company”), from comes, comitis (“companion”).

parole.significato: A state of agreement; harmony; union.
parole.testo: From French concorde, Latin concordia, from concors (“of the same mind, agreeing”); con- + cor, cordis (“heart”). See heart, and compare accord.

parole.significato: To agree; to act together.
parole.testo: From French concorder, from Latin concordō.

parole.significato: Agreeing or harmonious; consistent (with).
parole.testo: French concordant, from Latin concordans, present participle of concordare. See concord.

parole.significato: A formal agreement between two parties, especially between a church and a state; specifically, an agreement between the…
parole.testo: From French concordat, from Latin concordatum.

parole.significato: The process of aggregating or coalescing into a mass.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French concrétion, or Latin concretio.

parole.significato: A sudden solidification.
parole.testo: From French concours, from Latin concursus, from concurrere (“to run together”). See concur.

parole.significato: A smooth prominence on a bone where it forms a joint with another bone.
parole.testo: From French condyle, from Latin condylus, from Ancient Greek κόνδυλος (kóndulos, “knuckle”).

parole.significato: Any of various kinds of food that have been immersed in a substance for both flavor and preservation.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French confit, past participle of confire (“to preserve”), from Latin cōnficiō (perfect passive participle cōnfectus). Doublet of comfit, confect, confetto, and konfyt. Compare comfit.

parole.significato: A plant or animal of the same taxonomic genus as another.
parole.testo: From French congénère, from Latin com- (“same”) + genus (“kind”).

parole.significato: To collect (something) into a round mass; to conglobate.
parole.testo: PIE word  *ḱóm From French conglober, from Latin conglobāre, the present active infinitive of conglobō (“to gather into a ball; to accumulate; to crowd together”), from con- (prefix denoting a being or bringing together of several objects) + globus (“round object, globe, sphere; glob; group”) (from

parole.significato: Synonym of congius, Roman units of liquid measure and mass.
parole.testo: From French conge, from Latin congius, q.v. Only attested in English in the obsolete plural form congys.

parole.significato: To secretly cooperate with other people in order to commit a crime or other wrongdoing; to collude, to conspire.
parole.testo: From French conniver (“to ignore and thus become complicit in wrongdoing”), or directly from its etymon Latin con(n)īvēre (“close or screw up the eyes, blink, wink; overlook, turn a blind eye, connive”) (perhaps alluding to two persons involved in a scheme together winking to each other), from con-

parole.significato: Related by birth or "by blood", i.e. having close ancestors in common.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French consanguin. Doublet of consanguineous.

parole.significato: Able or likely to be consoled.
parole.testo: From console + -able. Derived from French consoler, from Latin consolari, which is from con- + solari (“to soothe”).

parole.significato: To comfort (someone) in a time of grief, disappointment, etc.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French consoler, from Latin cōnsōlor (“to console, offer solace”), root from Proto-Indo-European *selh₂- (“mercy, comfort”) (whence also solace).

parole.significato: Amazement or horror that confounds the faculties, and incapacitates for reflection; terror, combined with amazement; di…
parole.testo: From French consternation, from Latin consternātiō. By surface analysis, consternate + -ion.

parole.significato: A person or party that is consulted.
parole.testo: From French consultant, present participle of consulter, from Latin cōnsultāre (“to deliberate, consult”), frequentative of cōnsulere (“to consult, deliberate, consider, reflect upon, ask advice”), from com- (“together”) + -sulere, of uncertain origin.

parole.significato: Controversy; debate.
parole.testo: PIE word  *tréyes From French contester, from Old French, from Latin contestor (“to call to witness”).

parole.significato: Facing sinister instead of dexter.
parole.testo: From French contourné, from Latin con- (“altogether, completely”) and tornāre (“to make round”).

parole.significato: An abnormal, sometimes permanent, contraction of a muscle or skin; a deformity so caused.
parole.testo: From French contracture, from Latin contractura.

parole.significato: A difference in lightness, brightness or hue between two colours that makes them more or less distinguishable.
parole.testo: From French contraster, from Latin contrāstāre (“to resist", "to withstand”), from contrā (“against”) + stō, stāre (“to stand”).

parole.significato: A bruising of the brain caused by a blow, appearing on the opposite side to that on which the blow was struck.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French contrecoup, from contre (Latin contra) + coup a blow.

parole.significato: recovering one's health and strength after a period of illness; on the mend.
parole.testo: From French convalescent, from Latin convalēscēn(t-)s, present participle of convalēscere (“to become strong or well”); see convalesce.

parole.significato: Having elements of a feast or of entertainment, especially when it comes to eating and drinking, with accompanying fest…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French convivial, from Latin convīvium (“a feast”), combined form of con- (“together”) + vīvō (“to live”).

parole.significato: Of, relating to or pertaining to or resembling red algae of the family Corallinaceae.
parole.testo: From French corallin, from Latin corallinus, from corallium (“coral”), via Greek probably of Semitic origin. The taxonomic sense is a semantic loan from translingual Corallina and related terms. By surface analysis, coral + -ine.

parole.significato: A decorative basket for the display of flowers or fruits.
parole.testo: From French corbeil, from Latin corbicula, from corbis (“a basket”). Doublet of corbicula. By surface analysis, Latin corb- + -eil (“diminutive suffix”).

parole.significato: A feudal tax levied on horned cattle.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French cornage, from Latin cornū (“horn”) + -age.

parole.significato: A battlefield formation composed of two or more divisions.
parole.testo: From French corps d'armée (literally “army body”), from Latin corpus (“body”). Doublet of corpse and corpus. See also English riff.

parole.significato: Free from error; true; accurate.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French correct, from Latin correctus (“improved, amended, correct”), past participle of corrigere, conrigere (“to make straight, make right, make better, improve, correct”), from con- (“together”) + combining form of regō, regere (“I rule, make straight”).

parole.significato: The act of corrupting or of impairing integrity, virtue, or moral principle; the state of being corrupted or debased; l…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French corruption, from Latin corruptiō, equivalent to corrupt + -ion.

parole.significato: A material used for floor covering, made of ground cork and india rubber.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French corticine, from Latin cortex, corticis (“bark”).

parole.significato: A cluster of flowers with a flat or convex top.
parole.testo: From the French corymbe, from the Latin corymbus, from the Ancient Greek κόρυμβος (kórumbos). Doublet of corymbus.

parole.significato: Synonym of coryphaeus.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French coryphée, from Latin coryphaeus, from Ancient Greek κορυφαῖος (koruphaîos, “leader of the chorus in an Ancient Greek drama”), from κορῠφή (korŭphḗ, “top of the head, crown”) (possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱerh₂- (“head, top; horn”)) + -ῐος (-ĭos, suffix forming a

parole.significato: One who is at home in every place; a citizen of the world; a cosmopolitan person.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French cosmopolite, from Latin cosmopolītēs, itself borrowed from Koine Greek κοσμοπολίτης (kosmopolítēs, “citizen of the world”), from Ancient Greek κόσμος (kósmos, “world”) + πολίτης (polítēs, “citizen”).

parole.significato: A hilly upland including the divide between two valleys.
parole.testo: From French coteau, from Old French costel, from Latin costa (“rib, side”).

parole.significato: A particular variety of Cucurbita pepo, a small marrow/squash.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French courgette, diminutive of courge (“vegetable marrow, marrow squash”). Ultimately related to zucchini through Latin cucurbita.

parole.significato: Of a bird or other animal: to brood, cover, incubate, or sit over (eggs).
parole.testo: Borrowed from French couver, from Old French cover (“to hatch (eggs)”), from Latin cubāre (“to lie down, recline; to incubate; to be broody”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱewb- (“to lie down”). Cognates * Italian covare

parole.significato: To form into ringlets; to curl or crimp.
parole.testo: Alteration of French crepe, from Middle French crespe (“curly”), from Latin crispus. Doublet of crisp and crepe.

parole.significato: An usher to a riding master (riding instructor).
parole.testo: French, ultimately from Latin creatus (“created, begotten”); compare Italian creato (“pupil, servant”), Spanish criado (“a servant, client”).

parole.significato: A pattern along the top of a parapet (fortified wall), most often in the form of multiple, regular, rectangular spaces…
parole.testo: From crenellate + -ion (suffix indicating an action or process, or its result). Crenellate is derived from French créneler (“to form the shape of a crenel, crenellate”), from Old French crenel (“crenel, embrasure”) (modern French créneau) (from Latin *crēnella, diminutive of crēna (“incision; notch”

parole.significato: A flat round pancake-like pastry from Lower Brittany, made with wheat.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French crêpe, from Latin crispus. Doublet of crisp and crape.

parole.significato: A person who fails to develop mentally and physically due to a congenital hypothyroidism.
parole.testo: From French crétin (“cretin, idiot”), likely from crestin, an Alpine dialectal form of chrétien, from Latin christiānus in the lost sense of “anyone in Christendom”, often with a sense of “poor fellow”. Doublet of Christian.

parole.significato: The state of being criminal.
parole.testo: From French criminalité, from Latin criminalitas, from Latin criminalis. By surface analysis, criminal + -ity.

parole.significato: A mass-start road-cycle race consisting of several laps around a closed circuit, the length of each lap or circuit rang…
parole.testo: From French critérium (“competition”), from Latin critērium, from Ancient Greek κριτήριον (kritḗrion).

parole.significato: A flaky roll or pastry in a form of a crescent.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French croissant (“crescent”), present participle of croître (“to grow”). Doublet of crescent.

parole.significato: An artistic movement in the early 20th Century characterized by the depiction of natural forms as geometric structures…
parole.testo: From French cubisme. One story is that, in 1908, as a new canvas by Braque was being carried past, someone said, “Encore des cubes! assez de cubisme!”. parole.significato: Relating to the practice of cookery or the activity of cooking.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French culinaire, itself a borrowing from Latin culīnārius, from culīna (“kitchen”).

parole.significato: blameworthiness; fault
parole.testo: From French coulpe, from Latin culpa. Compare culpable, culprit.

parole.significato: The veneration, devotion, and religious rites given to a deity (especially in a historical polytheistic context), or (i…
parole.testo: Derived from French culte, from Latin cultus (“care, adoration; cult”), from colō (“cultivate; protect”).

parole.significato: Extreme greed, especially for wealth.
parole.testo: From French cupidité, from Latin cupiditās (“strong desire”), from cupidus (“keen, desirous”). Compare Cupid.

parole.significato: A thin slice of meat, usually fried.
parole.testo: From French côtelette (recorded in English since 1706), from Middle French costelette (“little rib”), from coste + -elette, from Old French coste (“rib, side”), from Latin costa. Influenced by English cut, as if from cut + -let. Doublet of kotlet and kotleta.

parole.significato: A zigzag or indented line or figure.
parole.testo: Apparently from a scribal error for French or Middle French denché, from Old French denché, dansié, from Latin dens (“tooth”).

parole.significato: To decide or determine (a matter disputed or doubtful), with simple object, with infinitive or object clause, or intran…
parole.testo: First attested in late Middle English circa 1425; from the French décerner, from the Latin dēcernō (“to decide, pronounce a decision”), from dē (“of, from, away from”) + cernō (“to separate, distinguish”), whence the English cern. In Old French, the forms of décerner were frequently conflated with t

parole.significato: The act or art of declaiming; rhetorical delivery; loud speaking in public.
parole.testo: From French déclamation, from Latin dēclāmātiō, dēclāmātiōnem, from dēclāmō, dēclāmāre; see declaim.

parole.significato: The downward slope of a curve.
parole.testo: 1610s, from French déclivité, from Latin declivitatem, dēclīvitās, from dēclivis (“a sloping downward”), from de (“down”) + clīvus (“a slope”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱleywo-, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱley- (“to lean”) (English lean).

parole.significato: The style of decoration of a room or building.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French décor.

parole.significato: To fail, or cause to fail.
parole.testo: French défaillir to fail; prefix dé- (Latin de) + faillir. See fail, and compare default.

parole.significato: Deficiency in amount or quality; a falling short; lack.
parole.testo: From French déficit, from Latin dēficit. Related to defect.

parole.significato: The process or state of growing worse, or the state of having become worse.
parole.testo: From French dégénération, from Latin dēgenerātiō.

parole.significato: tasting, especially as a form of careful appreciation
parole.testo: Borrowed from French dégustation, from Latin degustatio, degustationem, from degusto.

parole.significato: To make into a god.
parole.testo: From French déifier, from Latin deificāre, from deus (“god”). By surface analysis, deity + -ify.

parole.significato: Very fine in quality or luxurious.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French de luxe (“of luxury”), from Latin luxus (“excess”).

parole.significato: Resignation; abdication.
parole.testo: From French démission, from Latin dēmissiō, from dēmittō.

parole.significato: An old French coin worth one-twelfth of a sou.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French denier, from Latin dēnārius. Doublet of denar, denarius, dinar, diner, dinero, and dinheiro.

parole.significato: A tooth, as of a card, a gear wheel, etc.
parole.testo: From French dent, from Latin dēns, dentis (“tooth”). Doublet of dens and tooth.

parole.significato: A small tooth or toothlike structure.
parole.testo: From French denticule, from Latin denticulus. Doublet of denticle.

parole.significato: Any one of a series of small rectangular blocks projecting like teeth from a molding or beneath a cornice.
parole.testo: From French dentille, ultimately from Latin dente, ablative singular of dēns.

parole.significato: The hard, dense calcareous material that makes up the bulk of a tooth.
parole.testo: From French dentine, from Latin dens (“tooth”) + English chemical suffix -in / -ine.

parole.significato: A set of teeth, the teeth viewed as a unit.
parole.testo: From French denture (“set of teeth”), from Latin dens, dentis (“tooth”) + -urus, -ura, -urum, a suffix implying a set.

parole.significato: A lifelike image of something, either verbal or visual.
parole.testo: From French dépiction, from Latin dēpictiō. By surface analysis, depict + -ion.

parole.significato: To strip of feathers or plumage.
parole.testo: From French déplumer, from Latin dēplūmō, from dē- + plūmō (“to cover with feathers”), from plūma (“feather”). Compare dēplūmis (“featherless”).

parole.significato: To comport (oneself); to behave.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French déporter. With the meaning of "behave", from Old French deporter (“behave”), from Latin deportō, from de- + portō.

parole.significato: The removal of impurities, especially from bodily fluids; purification, cleansing.
parole.testo: From French dépuration or Latin deporationem, from depurare (“depurate”).

parole.significato: To assign (someone or something) to or for something.
parole.testo: From French députer, from Latin deputo.

parole.significato: To pull up by the roots; to uproot; to extirpate.
parole.testo: PIE word  *wréh₂ds First attested in 1609; calque of French déraciner on the basis of -ate (verb-forming suffix), from racine (“root”), from Latin rādīx, rādīcis (“a root”).

parole.significato: A female deserter.
parole.testo: From French désertrice, from Latin dēsertrīx, feminine form of desertor (“deserter”).

parole.significato: A suffix used as an inflection; an ending; inflectional suffix.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French désinence, from Latin dēsinentia, present participle of dēsinō (“to stop, end, close, make an end”).

parole.significato: That which locks or unlocks a movement; a catch (stopping mechanism), pawl, or dog; especially, in clockwork, the catch…
parole.testo: From French détente, from Latin tendō (“to stretch”).

parole.significato: To clean (especially a wound) of undesirable material.
parole.testo: From French déterger, from Latin dētergēre, from dē- + tergēre.

parole.significato: Any non-soap cleaning agent, especially a synthetic surfactant.
parole.testo: From French détergent, from Latin dētergēns, the present participle of dētergeō, from dē (“off”) + tergeō (“wipe, polish”).

parole.significato: To give up; to devote.
parole.testo: From French dévouer, Latin devovere. Equivalent to de- + vow. Doublet of devote (transitive verb).

parole.significato: Someone skilled in dialectics: someone able to arrive at logical conclusions through reasoned argument.
parole.testo: From French dialecticien (“one skillful in dialectic”), from Latin dialecticus (“dialectic”) + French -ien (“-ian”) from Latin -ianus (“-ian”). Equivalent to dialectic + -ian.

parole.significato: An abusive, bitter verbal or written attack, criticism or denunciation.
parole.testo: First attested 1581, borrowed from French diatribe, from Latin diatriba (“learned discussion or discourse”), from Ancient Greek διατριβή (diatribḗ, “way of spending time, lecture”), from διά (diá, “through”) + τρίβω (tríbō, “to waste, wear out”)

parole.significato: Of an animal: walking on the toes, putting the weight of the body mainly on the ball of the foot, with the back of the…
parole.testo: From French digitigrade, from Latin digitus (“finger, toe, digit”) + -grade (“gait”); compare New Latin digitigradus.

parole.significato: Steady application; industry; careful work involving long-term effort.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French diligence, from Latin diligentia.

parole.significato: The art and practice of conducting international relations by negotiating alliances, treaties, agreements etc., bilater…
parole.testo: From French diplomatie, a back-formation from diplomatique, ultimately from Latin diploma (“a letter of recommendation or authority”); see diploma.

parole.significato: A policy of strong state control over the economy and related social matters.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French dirigisme, from diriger (“to run, to direct”), from Latin dirigere (“direct, steer”).

parole.significato: Controlled or guided by a central authority, as in an economy.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French dirigiste, from diriger (“to run, to direct”), from Latin dirigere (“to direct, to steer”).

parole.significato: To harrow with a disc harrow.
parole.testo: From French disque, from Latin discus, from Ancient Greek δίσκος (dískos, “disk, quoit, platter”). Doublet of dais, desk, discus, dish, disk, and diskos.

parole.significato: To convey legal authority to another.
parole.testo: From French, from Latin disponĕre (“to arrange”).

parole.significato: A methodical inquiry or investigation.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French disquisition (“disquisition”), from Latin disquīsītiō (“inquiry, investigation”), from disquīrō (“to investigate”) (from dis- (prefix meaning ‘apart, asunder’) + quaerō (“to look for, seek; to inquire, question”)) + -tiō (suffix forming nouns relating to an action or the result

parole.significato: The act of dissociating or disuniting; a state of separation; disunion.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French dissociation, from Latin dissociātiō(n).

parole.significato: Comprising two syllables.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French dissyllabique, from Latin disyllabus, equivalent to di- + syllabic.

parole.significato: A motto or saying.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French dicton (“saying, maxim, proverb, adage”), from Latin dictum. First attested in the late 16th century.

parole.significato: The manner or character of a dogmatist; arrogance or positiveness in stating opinion.
parole.testo: From French dogmatisme, from Ecclesiastical Latin dogmatismus. Derived from Latin dogma (“philosophical tenet”), from Ancient Greek δόγμα (dógma, “opinion, tenet”), from δοκέω (dokéō, “to seem good, think”). Treated in the 17th and 18th century as Greek, with plural dogmata.

parole.significato: A cyclist on a cycle racing team whose role is to assist the team's designated leaders (for example, by riding in front…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French domestique (“domestic servant, maid”), from domestique (“domestic”, adjective), from Latin domesticus (“of the house, domestic; familiar; native”), from domus (“home, house; place of one's birth or residence, native country”). Doublet of domestic.

parole.significato: To bring (something) under control; to overcome, to subdue.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French dompter (“to break in, tame (an animal); to subdue, suppress”), from Middle French dompter, from Old French donter, danter, from Latin domitāre, the present active infinitive of domitō (“to tame”), from domō (“to break in, tame; to conquer, subdue, vanquish”) (ultimately from Pr

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Dorians.
parole.testo: Constructed like the French Doriens. From the Latin root of Dōres + -ian. Compare Ancient Greek Δωριεύς (Dōrieús, “of Doris”).

parole.significato: A move in square dancing in which two dancers face each other, then step forward and left until they have right shoulde…
parole.testo: From French dos à dos (“back to back”), from dos (“back”) (from Latin dorsum (“back”)) and à (from Latin ad (“to”).

parole.significato: A bib attached to the back of a cyclist's shirt that carries the cyclist's race number.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French dossard, from dos (“back (of a person)”) (ultimately from Latin dorsum (“back of the body”), further etymology uncertain) + -ard (suffix forming nouns indicating things belonging to or representing particular classes or sorts).

parole.significato: Sweetness of manner: agreeableness, gentleness.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French douceur (“sweetness”), from Old French dolçor, dulcur, etc., from Latin dulcōr + -em, from dulcis (“sweet”). Naturalized in Middle English as douceoure, dousour but treated as a French loanword from the 17th century onward. Doublet of dulcour.

parole.significato: Relaxing of tension, especially between countries; (countable) an instance of this.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French détente (“loosening, relaxing”), from Latin *dētendita, a feminine singular participle of dētendō (“to relax”), from dē- (prefix meaning ‘from; of’) + tendō (“to stretch”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *tend- (“to stretch”)).

parole.significato: Water.
parole.testo: From French eau, from Middle French eau, eaue, from Old French ewe, euwe, egua (“water”), from Latin aqua (“water”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ekʷeh₂ (“water, flowing water”). Doublet of aqua.

parole.significato: The state of intoxication, drunkenness.
parole.testo: From French ébriété (“drunkenness”), from Latin ēbrietātem, from ēbrius (“drunk”).

parole.significato: Synonym of ecclesiastical.
parole.testo: From French ecclésial, from Latin ecclēsiālis. By surface analysis, ecclesia + -al.

parole.significato: A level or rank in an organization, profession, or society.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French échelon (“rung; echelon”), from échelle (“ladder”) + -on (diminutive suffix). Échelle is derived from Latin scāla (“ladder”), from scandō (“to ascend, climb”), from Proto-Indo-European *skend- (“to jump”).

parole.significato: An animal of the phylum Echinodermata, comprising radially symmetric, spiny-skinned marine animals including seastars,…
parole.testo: From French échinoderme, corresponding to echino- + -derm, after plural of 18th-century Latin echinoderma.

parole.significato: ecology or the environment (in the ecological sense)
parole.testo: From French éco-, from Latin oeco-, from Ancient Greek οἶκος (oîkos, “house, household”).

parole.significato: A change to the text of a document.
parole.testo: Back-formation from editor, influenced by French éditer (“edit, publish”) and Latin editus.

parole.significato: A written work edited and published, as by a certain editor or in a certain manner, or at a certain time.
parole.testo: From French édition, from Latin ēditiō, from ēdere (“to publish”).

parole.significato: Having the power to produce a required effect or effects.
parole.testo: From French effectif, from Latin effectīvus (“productive; effective”), from efficiō (“to make; to bring about”), equivalent to effect + -ive.

parole.significato: A dummy or other crude representation of a person, group or object that is hated.
parole.testo: From French effigie, from Latin effigiēs (“likeness, effigy”), from effingō (“represent, portray”).

parole.significato: The production of flowers.

parole.significato: The process of flowing out.

parole.significato: A spray-like electric discharge.

parole.significato: An advocate of egoism.

parole.significato: The act of ejecting or suddenly throwing fluid or some other substance from a duct or other body structure.

parole.significato: To throw like a lance; to hurl.

parole.significato: An expression of praise.

parole.significato: The use of the lips, facial muscles, tongue, and teeth when playing a wind instrument.
parole.testo: From French embouchure, from emboucher (“to put in one’s mouth”), from en- (“in”) + bouche (“mouth”), from Latin bucca (“cheek”).

parole.significato: An agent sent on a mission to represent the interests of someone else.

parole.significato: A show; a program.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French émission.

parole.significato: Something which softens or lubricates the skin; moisturizer.

parole.significato: To cover with a hard crust.
parole.testo: From French incruster, from Latin incrustare, from in- (“in”) + crustare (“to cover with a crust”). By surface analysis, en- + crust.

parole.significato: To say or pronounce; to enunciate.
parole.testo: From French énoncer, from Latin ēnuntiō. Doublet of enunciate.

parole.significato: Between, in the process of, intermediate; inter-.

parole.significato: A sharp-pointed dueling sword with a bell-shaped guard, used (with the end blunted) in sport fencing.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French épée, from Latin spatha, from Ancient Greek σπάθη (spáthē). Doublet of spatha, spathe, and spade.

parole.significato: A follower or disciple.

parole.significato: A medical condition in which the sufferer experiences seizures (or convulsions) and blackouts.

parole.significato: The state of being calm, stable and composed, especially under stress.
parole.testo: From French équanimité, from Latin aequanimitās (“calmness, equanimity”), from aequus (“even; calm; fair”) + animus (“mind, soul”) + -itās. By surface analysis, equ- + anim(us) + -ity.

parole.significato: having equal power or force
parole.testo: From French équipollent, from Latin aequipollēns.

parole.significato: Capable of being raised to an upright position.

parole.significato: A logical deduction.
parole.testo: From French ergotisme, from Latin ergo.

parole.significato: To wear away by abrasion, corrosion, or chemical reaction.
parole.testo: From French éroder, from Latin ērōdō.

parole.significato: Relating to or tending to arouse sexual desire or excitement.
parole.testo: From French érotique, from Ancient Greek ἐρωτικός (erōtikós, “related to love”), from ἔρως (érōs, “sexual love”).

parole.significato: To make pale through lack of light, especially of a plant.
parole.testo: French étioler, from Norman French étieuler, ultimately from Old French estuble (“stubble”), from Latin stupla, from stipula (“straw, stubble”) (English stubble).

parole.significato: A short piece of music, designed to give a performer practice in a particular area or skill.
parole.testo: From around the year 1837, borrowed from French étude (“study”) from Latin studium. Doublet of studio and study.

parole.significato: Disappearing, vanishing.

parole.significato: The process of a liquid converting to the gaseous state.

parole.significato: Tending to avoid speaking openly or making revelations about oneself.
parole.testo: From French évasif, from Latin ēvādō.

parole.significato: To call out; to draw out or bring forth.

parole.significato: Attention to small details; accuracy.
parole.testo: From French exactitude, from exact, from Latin exactus, perfect passive participle of exigō (“demand, claim as due" or "measure by a standard, weigh, test”), from ex (“out”) + agō (“drive”).

parole.significato: To cut out; to remove.
parole.testo: From French exciser, from Latin excisus, past participle of excīdō (“cut out”), from ex (“out of, from”) + caedō (“cut”).

parole.significato: to be; have existence; have being or reality
