parole.significato: Very specific, clear, or detailed.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French explicite, from Latin explicitus (“disentangled, easy”), variant of explicātus.

parole.significato: The act of utilizing something; industry.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French exploitation, from exploiter (“exploit”), from Latin explicō (“unfold, deploy”). By surface analysis, exploit + -ation.

parole.significato: A violent release of energy (sometimes mechanical, nuclear, or chemical); an act or instance of exploding.
parole.testo: From French explosion, from Latin explōsiōnis, genitive form of explōsio, from explōdo (“to drive out by clapping”), from ex- and plōdo (“to clap or strike”). For more information see explode.

parole.significato: Moving or operating quickly, as a train not making local stops.
parole.testo: From French exprès, from Latin expressus, past participle of exprimere (see Etymology 2, below).

parole.significato: To exterminate (someone or something); to destroy.
parole.testo: From French exterminer, from Latin extermino.

parole.significato: To extirpate (something).
parole.testo: From French extirper, from Latin exstirpō (“to uproot”), from ex- (“out of”) + stirps (“the lower part of the trunk of a tree, including the roots; the stem, stalk”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix). Doublet of extirpate.

parole.significato: The outer or upper curve of an arch.
parole.testo: From French extradossé (“outer curve”) from Latin extra (“outside”) + dos (“back”) (from Latin dorsum).

parole.significato: Synonym of parfum (“solvent containing around 15% to 40% aromatic compounds”).
parole.testo: Borrowed from French extrait.

parole.significato: External; separable from the thing itself; inessential.
parole.testo: From French extrinsèque, from Latin extrinsecus (“from without, without, on the outside”), from *extrim, an assumed adverbial form of exter (“outer, outward”) + secus (“by, on the side”).

parole.significato: The quality of being exuberant; cheerful or vigorous enthusiasm; liveliness.
parole.testo: From French exubérance, from Latin exuberantia (“superabundance”), from exuberare (“to grow thickly, to abound”); from ex- (“out”) + uber (“udder”), which would have originally referred to a cow or she-goat which was making so much milk that it naturally dripped or sprayed from the udder.

parole.significato: An edifice or building.

parole.significato: Treating serious issues with (often deliberately) inappropriate humour; flippant.

parole.significato: To make easy or easier.

parole.significato: The act or manner of making or doing anything, especially of a literary, musical, or pictorial production.
parole.testo: From French facture (“a making, invoice”), from Latin factura (“a making”). Doublet of feature. See fact.

parole.significato: The state or quality of being feculent.

parole.testo: French; compare Old French ferrant (“iron-gray”), from Latin ferrum (“iron”).

parole.significato: A despicable fellow.

parole.testo: From French fractal, from Latin fractus (“broken”), perfect passive participle of frangō (“break, fragment”).

parole.significato: Forming terms relating to the fracture or breaking of something.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French fracto-, from Latin frāctus (“broken”).

parole.significato: A stylized strawberry with leaves.

parole.significato: Easily broken into small fragments, crumbled, or reduced to powder.

parole.significato: To behave frivolously.

parole.significato: To thunder or lightning.

parole.significato: The unpleasant odour or taste of old game meat.

parole.significato: A tightrope walker or a similar performer on a slack rope.

parole.significato: Causing death or disaster; fatal, catastrophic; deplorable, lamentable.

parole.significato: Synonym of fusil, a spindle-shaped figure.

parole.significato: An undesirable, difficult, or burdensome situation.

parole.significato: The necrosis and rotting of flesh, usually caused by lack of blood supply.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French gangrène, from Latin gangraena, from Ancient Greek γάγγραινα (gángraina, “gangrene”).

parole.significato: A servant boy or young waiter, particularly one who serves liquor.

parole.significato: A manufactured product of madder, used as a dye.

parole.significato: A kind; a stylistic category or sort, especially of literature or other artworks.

parole.significato: Affectedly proper or refined; somewhat prudish refinement; excessively polite.

parole.significato: Non-Jewish.

parole.significato: A nodule of stone having a cavity lined with mineral or crystal matter on the inside wall.

parole.significato: The quality or state of being gigantic; being of abnormally large size.
parole.testo: From French gigantisme, from Latin gigans (“giant”).

parole.significato: Of, or relating to glaciers.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French glacial, from Latin glaciālis, from glaciēs (“ice”). The sense "slow" refers to the speed of actual glaciers, typically around 1 meter per day.

parole.significato: Characteristic, composed, or of the nature of icy; icy.
parole.testo: From obsolete French glacieux, from Latin glaciēs (“ice”).

parole.significato: A gentle incline.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French glacis (“slippery surface”), derived from Old French glacier (“to glide; freeze”), the former from Latin glaciāre (“to freeze”), from glaciēs (“ice”), of uncertain origin. Cognates * Medieval Latin glatia (“incline in front of a fortification”)

parole.significato: A specialized cell, group of cells, or organ of endothelial origin in the human or animal body that synthesizes a chemi…
parole.testo: Late 17th century borrowing from French glande, alteration of Old French glandre, from Latin glandulae (“throat glands, tonsils”), plural of glandula (“a little acorn”), from glāns (“an acorn”) + -ula (diminutive nominal suffix).

parole.significato: Pertaining to a gland or glands.
parole.testo: Mid 18th century borrowing from French glandulaire, from glandule (“small gland”) + -aire (“-ar, -ary”, adjectival suffix), from Latin glandulae (“glands of the throat”); equivalent to glandule + -ar.

parole.significato: A small round particle of substance; a drop.
parole.testo: From French globule, from Latin globulus, from globus (“globe”).

parole.significato: An object such as a pillar or a rod that is used to tell time by the shadow it casts when the sun shines on it, especia…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French gnomon, or directly from its etymon Latin gnōmōn, or directly from its etymon Ancient Greek γνώμων (gnṓmōn, “discerner, interpreter; carpenter’s square; gnomon of a sundial; (geometry) gnomon”), from γιγνώσκω (gignṓskō, “to be aware of; to perceive; to know”), ultimately from Pr

parole.significato: A pool in a cave confined by a dam of mineral deposits accumulating along its rim.
parole.testo: From French gour (“rock pool”), from Latin gurges. Doublet of gorge and gurges.

parole.significato: A tiny grain, a small particle.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French granule or directly from Late Latin grānulum, diminutive of Latin grānum (“grain”); for more, see grain. By surface analysis, grain + -ule.

parole.significato: To please.
parole.testo: From French gratifier, from Latin grātificō (“to do a favor to, oblige, please, gratify”), from grātus (“kind, pleasing”) + faciō (“to make”).

parole.significato: To cook (food) on a grill; to barbecue.
parole.testo: 1655, from French gril, from Middle French gril, from Old French greïl, graïl (“gridiron”), from graïlle (“grate, grating”), from Latin crātīcula (“gridiron”), diminutive of crātis (“hurdle, wickerwork”), q.v. Related to griddle, hurdle.

parole.significato: A book of instructions in the use of alchemy or magic, especially one containing spells for summoning demons.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French grimoire, a variant of grammaire, from Old French gramaire (“grammar; grimoire; conjurer, magician”), from Latin grammatica (“grammar; philology”), from grammaticus (“relating to grammar, grammatical”), from Ancient Greek γρᾰμμᾰτῐκός (grămmătĭkós, “knowing one's letters; concern

parole.significato: One of a school of ancient Indian ascetic philosophers, reported in antiquity, who wore little clothing; a mystic.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French gymnosophiste, from Latin gymnosophista, from Ancient Greek γυμνοσοφιστής (gumnosophistḗs), from γυμνός (gumnós, “naked”) + σοφιστής (sophistḗs, “sophist”).

parole.significato: Any of various papilionid butterflies of the genus Papilio.
parole.testo: From French Hélène, from Latin Helena, from Ancient Greek Ἑλένη (Helénē). Doublet of Elaine.

parole.significato: A plant with flowers which turn to face and follow the sun, such as (archaic) marigolds and sunflowers.
parole.testo: PIE word  *sóh₂wl̥ The noun is borrowed from French héliotrope, from Latin hēliotropium (“plant which turns to face the sun; bloodstone”), from Ancient Greek ἡλῐοτρόπῐον (hēlĭotrópĭon, “European heliotrope (Heliotropium europaeum); bloodstone; solar clock, sundial”), from ἥλῐος (hḗlĭos, “the sun”) (

parole.significato: An approximate half-line of verse, separated from another by a caesura, often for dramatic effect.
parole.testo: From French hémistiche, from Latin hēmistichium, from Ancient Greek ἡμιστίχιον (hēmistíkhion), from ἡμι- (hēmi-, “half”) + στίχος (stíkhos, “verse”).

parole.significato: An Old World plant (Paris quadrifolia) related to the trillium.
parole.testo: From French herbe paris, from Latin par (“equal”), in reference to the regularity of its leaves, petals, etc. See image.

parole.significato: An organism that feeds chiefly on plants; an animal that feeds on herbage or vegetation as the main part of its diet.
parole.testo: From French herbivore, from Latin herbivorus. By surface analysis, herb (“herbage”) + -i- + -vore.

parole.significato: A writing system of ancient Egypt, Minoans, Maya and other civilizations, using pictorial symbols to represent individu…
parole.testo: First coined 1726, from French hiéroglyphique, from Latin hieroglyphicus, from Ancient Greek ἱερογλυφικός (hierogluphikós), from ἱερογλυφέω (hierogluphéō, “to represent hieroglyphically”), from ἱερός (hierós, “sacred, holy”) + γλύφω (glúphō, “to carve, to engrave, to cut out”). By surface analysis,

parole.significato: A horse racing course.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French hippodrome, a learned borrowing from Latin hippodromos, borrowed from Ancient Greek ῐ̔ππόδρομος (hĭppódromos), from ῐ̔́ππος (hĭ́ppos, “horse”) + δρόμος (drómos, “street”). By surface analysis, hippo- + -drome.

parole.significato: A lodging for pilgrims or the destitute, normally provided by a monastic order.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French hospice, from Old French hospise, from Latin hospitium (“hospitality, an inn”). Doublet of hospitium.

parole.significato: Of, from or relating to the Hyblaean Mountains in southeastern Sicily, Italy.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French Hybléen, via Latin hyblaeus, ultimately from Ancient Greek ὑβλαῖος (hublaîos, “Hyblaean”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to water.
parole.testo: From French hydraulique, from Latin hydraulicus, from Ancient Greek ὑδραυλικός (hudraulikós, “of a water organ”), from ὕδραυλις (húdraulis, “water organ”), from ὕδωρ (húdōr, “water”) + αὐλός (aulós, “pipe”).

parole.significato: An abnormal build-up of fluids at a site in the body, especially in the membranes around a testicle.
parole.testo: From French hydrocèle or Latin hydrocēlē, from Ancient Greek ὑδροκήλη (hudrokḗlē), from ὕδωρ (húdōr, “water”) + κήλη (kḗlē, “tumour”).

parole.significato: Divination by water or other liquid.
parole.testo: From French hydromancie or Late Latin hydromantia, from Ancient Greek ὑδρομαντεία (hudromanteía); corresponding to hydro- + -mancy.

parole.significato: A hydrophobic compound or material.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French hydrophobe, from Latin hydrophobus, from Ancient Greek ὑδροφόβος (hudrophóbos), from ὑδρο- (hudro-, “water”) + φόβος (phóbos, “fear, dread”).

parole.significato: Shaped like a U, or like the letter upsilon (υ).
parole.testo: Borrowing from French hyoïde, from New Latin hȳoīdēs, from Ancient Greek ῡ̔οειδής (hūoeidḗs, “shaped like the letter "υ"”), from ὖ (û, “the Greek letter upsilon”) + -ο- (-o-) + -ειδής (-eidḗs, “-like, -oid”).

parole.significato: I am able to think, therefore I exist; a proof of existence based on the fact that someone capable of any form of thoug…
parole.testo: Calque of French je pense, donc je suis or perhaps of Latin cōgitō, ergō sum. First written in French by René Descartes, a 17th century French philosopher, in Discourse on the Method (1637) as je pense donc je suis, which he later expressed in Latin in Principles of Philosophy (1644).

parole.significato: A metrical foot in verse consisting of an unstressed syllable followed by a stressed syllable.
parole.testo: From French iambe in the mid-1800s, from Latin ïambus, from Ancient Greek ἴαμβος (íambos). Displaced iambus which shares the same classical origin.

parole.significato: A freshwater fish of the family Cyprinidae, found across northern Europe and Asia, especially Leuciscus idus.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French ide, from Scientific Latin idus (species name), from Swedish id.

parole.significato: Great dishonor, shame, or humiliation.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French ignominie, from Latin ignōminia, from ig- (“not”) + nomen (“name”) (prefix assimilated form of in-).

parole.significato: To deliberately not listen or pay attention to.
parole.testo: From French ignorer, from Latin ignōrō (“to have no knowledge of, mistake, take no notice of, ignore”), from ignārus (“not knowing”), from in- (“not”) + gnārus (“knowing”), from gnōscō, nōscō; see know.

parole.significato: Relating to the ilium.
parole.testo: From French iliaque, from Late Latin īliacus, Latin īlium.

parole.significato: Not approved by law, but not invalid.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French illicite, from Latin illicitus, from in- (“not”) + licitus (“allowed, permitted”), from licet (“it is allowed”). By surface analysis, il- + licit.

parole.significato: Beardless.
parole.testo: From French imberbe, from Latin imberbis.

parole.significato: A set of tiles or shingles that overlap like the scales of a fish.
parole.testo: From French imbrication, from Latin imbricātus, from imbricō, from imbrex. By surface analysis, imbricate + -ion.

parole.significato: Capable of being imitated or copied.
parole.testo: From French imitable, from Latin imitābilis. See imitate.

parole.significato: A person who imitates or apes another.
parole.testo: From French imitateur, derived from Latin imitātor, equivalent to imitate + -or.

parole.significato: Not personal; not representing a person; not having personality.
parole.testo: From French impersonnel, from Latin impersōnālis, from im- (“not”) + persōnālis (“personal”), equivalent to im- + personal.

parole.significato: The action of imploring; begging, beseeching.
parole.testo: From French imploration, from Latin implorationem.

parole.significato: The condition of being improper.
parole.testo: From French impropriété, from Latin improprietās. By surface analysis, improper + -iety or im- + propriety.

parole.significato: To make something up or invent it as one goes on; to proceed guided only by imagination, intuition, and guesswork rathe…
parole.testo: From French improviser; ultimately from Latin improvisus.

parole.significato: Not active, temporarily or permanently.
parole.testo: From French inactif. Piecewise doublet of unactive.

parole.significato: The property of being inane, of lacking material of interest or satisfaction, emptiness.
parole.testo: From French inanité, from Latin inānitās (“emptiness”), equivalent to inane + -ity.

parole.significato: Of inauguration; as in a speech or lecture by the person being inaugurated.
parole.testo: From French inaugural, from inaugurer, from Latin augurare (“to take omens”).

parole.significato: Emitting light as a result of being heated.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French incandescent, from Latin incandescens, from incandesco (“be heated, glow”), from in- (intensifying prefix) + candesco (“become white”), from candidus (“white”).

parole.significato: Beginning; of or relating to inception.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French inceptif, from the Latin inceptīvus, from incipiō (“to begin”).

parole.significato: A call to act; encouragement to act, often in an illegal way.
parole.testo: From French incitement, from Latin incitāmentum (“incentive; incitement”), from incitō (“urge; quicken; incite”, verb). Equivalent to incite + -ment.

parole.significato: To make (someone) uncomfortable; to discomfort, to disturb, to trouble.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from French incommoder (“to bother, disconcert, incommode”), from Latin incommodāre, the present active infinitive of incommodō (“to inconvenience”), from in- (prefix meaning ‘not’) + commodō (“to accommodate, adapt; to bestow, provide; to hire, lend”) (from com- (a variant of con-

parole.significato: Synonym of incommodious.
parole.testo: The adjective is a learned borrowing from French incommode (“causing discomfort; inconvenient; troublesome; undesirable, unwanted, unwelcome”), from Latin incommodus (“inconvenient; disagreeable, troublesome; unfit, unsuitable, unseasonable”), from in- (prefix meaning ‘not’) + commodus (“becoming, s

parole.significato: The time elapsed between an exposure to a pathogenic organism, a chemical or radiation, and the appearance of signs and…
parole.testo: Since 1850s, from earlier period of incubation, attested in that now obsolete sense since late 1820s, which is a calque of French période d'incubation (attested since mid-1810s), itself a calque from Latin periodus incubationis (attested since 1770s).

parole.significato: That one cannot decline; unavoidable.
parole.testo: From French indéclinable, from Middle French, from Latin indeclinabilis. Equivalent to in- + declinable.

parole.significato: That cannot be told; indescribable, inexpressible, unspeakable.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from French inénarrable, from Latin inēnārrābilis (“indescribable”), from in- (prefix meaning ‘not’) + ēnārrābilis (“describable, explainable”). parole.significato: Unable to move or act; inanimate.
parole.testo: From French inerte, from Latin iners (“inactive, inert”).

parole.significato: The murder of an infant.
parole.testo: From French infanticide, from Latin īnfanticīdium. By surface analysis, infant + -i- + -cide.

parole.significato: The murderer of a child: a person who has committed infanticide.
parole.testo: From French infanticide, from Latin īnfanticīda. By surface analysis, infant + -i- + -cide.

parole.significato: An innocent, unsophisticated, naive, wholesome boy or young man.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French ingénu (“guileless”), especially as used by Voltaire in L'Ingénu, from Latin ingenuus (“ingenuous”). Doublet of ingenuous.

parole.significato: Unappetizingly flavorless.
parole.testo: From French insipide, from Latin īnsipidus (“tasteless”), from in- (“not”) + sapidus (“savory”). In some senses, perhaps influenced by insipient (“unwise, foolish, stupid”).

parole.significato: The incident radiant energy emitted by the sun which reaches a unit area over a period of time, typically measured over…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French insolation, from Latin insolatio (“a setting or placing in the sun”).

parole.significato: An organization founded to promote a cause
parole.testo: From French institut, from Middle French, from Latin īnstitūtum.

parole.significato: Any molecule that intercalates, or is inserted, between two others
parole.testo: Borrowed from French intercalant, from Latin intercalantem, accusative of intercalans.

parole.significato: The act of interdicting or something interdicted.
parole.testo: From Middle English, borrowed from French interdiction, itself a borrowing from Latin interdictiō.

parole.significato: A decree of a court.
parole.testo: From French interlocutoire, from Latin interlocūtōrium.

parole.significato: A short musical dramatic piece, of a light, pleasing, and sometimes burlesque character.
parole.testo: From French intermède, from Latin inter (“between”) + medius (“middle”). Compare Italian intermedio. Doublet of intermezzo.

parole.significato: A person who is interned, forcibly or voluntarily.
parole.testo: From French interner, from interne (“inner, internal”), from Latin internus (“within, internal”), compare Etymology 2.

parole.significato: A student or recent graduate who works in order to gain experience in their chosen field.
parole.testo: From French interne (“inner, internal”), from Latin internus (“within, internal”), from inter (“between”); compare Etymology 1.

parole.significato: An abrupt change in elements, with continuation of the first idea.
parole.testo: From French interpolation, from Latin interpolatio. Morphologically interpolate + -ion.

parole.significato: The state of being intolerant.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French intolérance, itself from in- (“not”) + tolérance or borrowed from Latin intolerantia (“insolence, insufferableness; (very rare) intolerance”). By surface analysis, in- + tolerance.

parole.significato: Fearless; bold; brave.
parole.testo: From French intrépide, from Latin intrepidus, from in- (“not”) + trepidus (“anxious, nervous”).

parole.significato: The invagination of one portion of a tubular anatomical structure (especially intestines or blood vessels) within the n…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French intussusception, or directly from Latin intussusceptiō, from intus (“within”) + susceptiō (“susception”).

parole.significato: Conspicuous bract, bract pair or ring of bracts at the base of an inflorescence.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French involucre, from Latin involūcrum (“wrapper”). Doublet of involucrum.

parole.significato: The state of being irreligious; irreligious sentiment or thought.
parole.testo: From French irréligion, from Latin irreligiō. By surface analysis, ir- + religion.

parole.significato: Capable of being irritated.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French irritable, from Latin irritabilis.

parole.significato: Veined or clouded like imitation jasper.
parole.testo: From French jaspé, past participle of jasper (“to colour motley, so as to imitate jasper”), from jaspe (“jasper”), from Latin iaspis, from Ancient Greek ἴασπις (íaspis).

parole.significato: A long speech or prose work that bitterly laments the state of society and its morals, and often contains a prophecy of…
parole.testo: From French jérémiade, from Jérémie, from Latin Ieremias, from Hebrew ירמיה (yirm'yá, “Jeremiah”). Named after biblical prophet Jeremiah, who lamented the moral state of Judah and predicted her downfall.

parole.significato: The houseleek.
parole.testo: From the French joubarbe, jousbarbe, from the Latin Iovis barba (“Jove's beard”).

parole.significato: Having, characterized by, or done with good judgment or sound thinking.
parole.testo: From French judicieux, ultimately derived from Latin iudico. Related to judge, judicial.

parole.significato: To place side by side, especially for contrast or comparison.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French juxtaposer, corresponding to juxta- + pose, derived from Latin iuxtā (“near, next to”) + pōnō (“place”).

parole.significato: The nearness of objects with little or no delimiter.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French juxtaposition, from Latin iuxtā (“near”) (from Latin iungō (“to join”)) + French position (“position”) (from Latin pōnō (“to place”)).

parole.significato: A layperson as opposed to a cleric, i.e. not a member of the clergy.
parole.testo: From French laïque, from Latin lāicus (“common people”), from Ancient Greek λαός (laós). Doublet of lay.

parole.significato: Having a group of flat lamellae on the end.
parole.testo: From French lamellicorne, from Latin lamella (“a thin plate”) + cornu (“a horn”).

parole.significato: Small steel plates combined so as to slide one upon other and form a piece of armour: plural of lame.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French lame (“a thin plate”), from Latin lāmina.

parole.significato: A soft, pungent cow's-milk cheese with a washed rind, from the Langres region of France.
parole.testo: From French Langres, from Latin Lingones, a Gaulish tribe who lived in the area.

parole.significato: A tearpit (in animals)
parole.testo: From French larme (“tear, drop”), from Latin lacrima. See lachrymose.

parole.significato: Lethargy or lack of energy; fatigue, languor, listlessness
parole.testo: Borrowed from French lassitude, from Latin lassitūdō (“faintness, weariness”), from lassus (“faint, weary”), perhaps for *ladtus, and thus akin to English late.

parole.significato: An open trench or pit used for urination and defecation.
parole.testo: From French latrine (“latrine”), from Latin lātrīna.

parole.significato: A type of thin linen or cotton fabric tightly woven of fine threads. (Traditionally expensive and luxurious in centurie…
parole.testo: Apparently from Laon, a French town known for its linen manufacturing, from Old French Lan, from Latin Laudunum, a Celtic name cognate with Lugdunum.

parole.significato: The fruit or seed of leguminous plants (as peas or beans) used for food.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French légume, from Latin legūmen (“bean”). Doublet of legumen.

parole.significato: A low-relief, vertical pillar or pilaster in a wall, usually without a base or capital; used in architecture to divide…
parole.testo: From French lisse, from Latin licium (“thread, loop”).

parole.significato: An easterly wind, generally in the western Mediterranean Sea.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French levant (“rising, sun's point of rising”), form of lever (“to rise”), from Latin levō (“to rise”) (cf. also the present participle levāns), from levis (“light, not heavy”).

parole.significato: A disappearing or absconding after losing a bet.
parole.testo: Transferral use of Levant, from French levant. Compare French faire voile en Levant (“to sail eastward”), literally: set the sail with the Levant, an easterly wind that blows in the Mediterranean Sea. Ultimately from Latin levō + -ant.

parole.significato: A thickening for sauces, typically based on egg yolks.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French liaison (“binding”), from Latin ligātiō (stem ligātiōn-; whence the English doublet ligation), derived from ligō (“to bind”), from Proto-Indo-European *leyǵ- (“to bind”).

parole.significato: A plane curve with polar equation ρ=a+b, sin ,θ or ρ=a+b, cos ,θ, of which the cardioid is a special case.
parole.testo: From French limaçon, ultimately from Latin limax (“snail”).

parole.significato: Relating to the limbic system.
parole.testo: From French limbique, from Latin limbus (“edge, border”).

parole.significato: Introductory or preparatory.
parole.testo: From French liminaire (“introductory”) from Latin līmināris, from līmen (“doorstep, threshold; doorway, entrance; beginning, commencement”) + -ālis (suffix forming adjectives of relationship from nouns). Līmen is possibly derived from līmus (“askew; sideways”) (possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-Eu

parole.significato: Border, frontier; being or existing along a border or frontier.
parole.testo: From French limitrophe, from Latin limitrophus.

parole.significato: One of a breed of cattle from this region.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French Limousin, from Latin Lemovicinus, adjective form of Lemovices, name of a Gaulish tribe in central France, most likely a reference to their elm bows and spears, of same ultimate origin as elm.

parole.significato: Clear, transparent or bright.
parole.testo: From French limpide, from Latin limpidus.

parole.significato: The property of being limpid.
parole.testo: From French limpidité, from Latin limpiditas.

parole.significato: A shoemaker's thread rubbed with beeswax.
parole.testo: French ligneul, diminutive of Latin linea (“a linen thread”).

parole.significato: A fine sheer fabric of silk or cotton used in women's neckwear and in ruching.
parole.testo: From French lisse, from Latin licium.

parole.significato: A party suing or being sued in a lawsuit, or otherwise calling upon the judicial process to determine the outcome of a…
parole.testo: From French litigant, from Middle French, from Latin litigans.

parole.significato: A person engaged in various literary works: literary critic, essayist, writer.
parole.testo: From the French littérateur, from the Latin litterātor (“critic”). Doublet of literator.

parole.significato: The ability to move from place to place, or the act of doing so.
parole.testo: From French locomotion, from Latin locō (literally “from a place”) (ablative of locus (“place”)) + mōtiōnem (“motion, a moving”) (nominative mōtio), from Latin movēre (“move; change, exchange, go in or out, quit”), from Proto-Indo-European *m(y)ewh₁- (“to move, drive”).

parole.significato: The power unit of a train that pulls the coaches or wagons.
parole.testo: From French locomotif, from Latin locō (literally “from a place”) (ablative of locus (“place”)) + Vulgar Latin mōtivus (“moving”) (see motive). In the rail transport sense, ellipsis of locomotive (steam) engine, attested from 1814.

parole.significato: To work (a horse) in a circle at the end of a long line or rope.
parole.testo: From French allonger (“to lengthen”), or Latin longa (“long”), i.e. the long rope.

parole.significato: Degree of ability to lubricate.
parole.testo: From French lubricité or its source, Latin lūbricitās.

parole.significato: Producing a surplus; profitable.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French lucratif, from Latin lucrativus (“profitable”), from lucratus, past participle of lucror (“to gain”), from lucrum (“gain”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *leh₂w- (“profit, gain”). Compare Spanish lucrar. By surface analysis, lucre + -ative.

parole.significato: Playful.
parole.testo: From French ludique, from Latin ludo (“to play”).

parole.significato: A concave figure formed by the intersection of the arcs of two circles on a plane, or on a sphere the intersection betw…
parole.testo: From French lune, from Latin luna.

parole.significato: Anything crescent-shaped; a crescent-shaped part or mark; a lunula or lune.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French lunule, from Latin lūnula, diminutive of lūna (“moon”). By surface analysis, luna + -ule.

parole.significato: A dormer-window.
parole.testo: From French lucarne (“a dormer, dormer window, garret window”), Latin lucerna (“lamp”), from lucere (“to be light or clear”), from lux (“light”).

parole.significato: Luxury.
parole.testo: From French luxe, from Latin luxus. Cognate with English lock.

parole.significato: Pure water.
parole.testo: Borrowing from French lymphe and/or Latin lympha (“clear water”), from Ancient Greek νῠ́μφη (nŭ́mphē, “bride; spring water”). Doublet of nymph.

parole.significato: Of, or relating to a type of poetry (such as a sonnet or ode) that expresses subjective thoughts and feelings, often in…
parole.testo: From French lyrique, or its source, Latin lyricus, from Ancient Greek λυρικός (lurikós), from λύρα (lúra, “lyre”). Its English equivalent would be lyre + -ic. The original Greek sense of "lyric poetry"—"poetry accompanied by the lyre" i.e. "words set to music"—eventually led to its use as "lyrics",

parole.significato: The crime of violating majesty, an offense against the dignity of a reigning sovereign or against a state.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French lèse-majesté, from Latin laesa maiestās (“injured majesty”).

parole.significato: A constructor of machines and engines; someone knowledgeable about machines.
parole.testo: From French machiniste, from machine (“machine, mechanical device”), from Latin māchina, from Ancient Greek μηχανή (mēkhanḗ, “machine”).

parole.significato: A palindromic square word arrangement, usually in the form of a magic amulet.
parole.testo: As magical square by 1670 and magic square by 1701 (see Citations). Calque of French quarré magique or Latin quadratum magicum. Magic refers to its original function as a talisman.

parole.significato: A capital letter, especially one used in ancient manuscripts.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French majuscule, from Latin majuscula (littera).

parole.significato: A crusty rash in the bend of the knee of the foreleg of a horse.
parole.testo: French malandres, from Latin malandria (“blisters or pustules on the neck, especially in horses”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to apples.
parole.testo: From French malique, from Latin mālum.

parole.significato: Corrupt behaviour, illegitimate activity, especially by someone in authority.
parole.testo: From French malversation, from malverser, from Latin male versari (“behave badly”). Compare Spanish malversación (“embezzlement”).

parole.significato: The practice of manipulating or the state of being manipulated.
parole.testo: From French manipulation, from Old French manipule, from Latin manipulus. Morphologically manipulate + -ion.

parole.significato: Maintenance, upkeep of a person, place or thing.
parole.testo: From French manutention, from Latin manutentio (“maintenance”), from present participle of manutenere (“to maintain”).

parole.significato: A towel used by a priest during liturgy.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French manuterge, from Latin manutergium, from manus (“hand”) + tergeō (“wipe, clean”) + -ium.

parole.significato: A thin silk fabric used for linings etc. in hats and ladies' dresses.
parole.testo: From French marceline, from Latin marcidus (“withered”), from marcere (“to wither, shrivel”).

parole.significato: Margin; edge; brink or verge.
parole.testo: From French marge, from Latin margo. Doublet of margin and margo.

parole.significato: Relating to mass.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French massique, from Latin massicus, from massa (“mass”). By surface analysis, mass + -ic.

parole.significato: A principal mountain mass.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French massif, from Middle French massif, ultimately from Latin massa, from Ancient Greek μᾶζα (mâza, “barley-cake, lump (of dough)”).

parole.significato: The state of being a mother; motherhood.
parole.testo: From French maternité, from Latin māternitās.

parole.significato: The killing of one's mother.
parole.testo: From French matricide, from Latin mātricīda (“person who kills his own mother”) and mātricīdium (“the murder of one's mother”). By surface analysis, matri- + -cide.

parole.significato: A rich purple synthetic dye, which faded easily, briefly popular c. 1859‒1873 and now called mauveine.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French mauve (“mallow”), from Latin malva, which has a purple colour. Doublet of mallow. Coined in 1856 by the chemist William Henry Perkin, when he accidentally created the first aniline dye.

parole.significato: The highest limit.
parole.testo: Via French from Latin maximum.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Middle Ages, the period from approximately 500 to 1500 AD.
parole.testo: From French médiéval (“medieval”), from Latin medium (“middle”) + aevum (“age”).

parole.significato: Not excellent or outstanding, usually disappointingly so.
parole.testo: From the late Middle English medioker, from the French médiocre, from the Middle French médiocre, from the Classical Latin mediocris (“in a middle state”, “of middle size”, “middling”, “moderate”, “ordinary”, from medius (“middle”) + ocris (“rugged mountain”)); compare mediocrely and mediocrity.

parole.significato: A battle fought at close range, (especially) one not involving ranged weapons; hand-to-hand combat; brawling.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French mêlée, from Old French meslee, feminine past participle of mesler (“to mix”), derived from Latin misceō (“mix”). Doublet of medley.

parole.significato: An autobiography; a book describing the personal experiences of an author.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French mémoire, from Middle French memoire, from Old French memoire, from Latin memoria. Doublet of memoria and memory.

parole.significato: Synonym of menologium, a monthly record, particularly in certain Christian contexts
parole.testo: From French ménologe, from Latin mēnologium, q.v. Doublet of menologion, menologium, and menology.

parole.significato: Ordure; dung, shit, excrement.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French merde and Latin merda. Doublet of mierda and merde.

parole.significato: Of a moth or insect, to undergo metamorphosis.
parole.testo: From French métamorphoser, from Old French metamorphose, from Latin metamorphōsis; see metamorphosis.

parole.significato: Vertically divided into distinctly-coloured or patterned halves; party per pale.
parole.testo: The adjective is a learned borrowing from French mi-parti (literally “divided down the middle”), from Middle French mi-parti, from Old French mi-parti, an adjective use of the past participle of mi-partir (“to split in half”), from mi- (prefix meaning ‘half’) + partir (“to divide up”): * Mi- is from

parole.significato: An environment or setting; a medium; environs
parole.testo: PIE word  *me Borrowed from French milieu (“physical or social environment; group of people with a common point of view”), from Middle French milieu, meilleu, mileu, from Old French milliu, meillieu, mileu (“middle”), from mi- (prefix meaning ‘half’) (from Latin medius (“half; middle”)) + lieu, leu

parole.significato: Any coral of the genus Millepora, having the surface nearly smooth, and perforated with very minute unequal pores, or c…
parole.testo: From French millépore, from Latin mille (“thousand”) + porus (“pore”).

parole.significato: In the International System of Units and other metric systems of units, one-thousandth of the unit to which it is prefi…
parole.testo: From Latin mille (“thousand”), via French.

parole.significato: A slow graceful dance consisting of a coupé, a high step, and a balance.
parole.testo: From French menuet, from menu (“small”) + -et (“diminutive”), from Latin minutus (“very small”).

parole.significato: A lowercase letter.
parole.testo: From French minuscule, from Latin minuscula, feminine of minusculus (“rather less, rather small”), from minus (“less, smaller”) + -culus (diminutive suffix).

parole.significato: A grammatical mood that expresses (surprise at) unexpected revelations or new information.
parole.testo: Possibly from (ad)mirative, from French admiratif (“tending to admire”) (used by French diplomat and scholar Auguste Dozon (1822–1890), imitating the use of the Ancient Greek ἀπροσδόκητος (aprosdókētos, “unexpected”) in a similar context by Albanian translator and scholar Kostandin Kristoforidhi (18

parole.significato: An assortment of miscellaneous items.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French miscellanées, from Latin mīscellānea, from miscellus (“mixed”), from misceō (“to mix”).

parole.significato: A self-contained component of a system, often interchangeable, which has a well-defined interface to the other componen…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French module, from Latin modulus (“a small measure, a measure, mode, meter”), diminutive of modus (“measure”) (whence mode). Doublet of modulus and mold.

parole.significato: The base with respect to which a congruence is computed.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from French module as Latin modulus. Doublet of module and mold.

parole.significato: An unguent for the hair.
parole.testo: French moelle, from Latin medulla (“marrow”).

parole.significato: A shallow deposit of sandstone, shale and conglomerate in front of a rising mountain chain.
parole.testo: From French molasse, a kind of sandstone, from Latin mollis (“soft”).

parole.significato: A massive structure, usually of stone, used as a pier, breakwater or junction between places separated by water.
parole.testo: From French môle or Latin mōles (“mass, heap, rock”).

parole.significato: A hemorrhagic mass of tissue in the uterus caused by a dead ovum.
parole.testo: In English since before the 20th century. From French môle f, from Latin mola (“millstone”), because it is a hardened mass.

parole.significato: A kind of thick woollen material, once important in the Canada trade.
parole.testo: French molleton, from molle + -et (“diminutive”) + -on (“diminutive”), from Latin mollis (“soft”).

parole.significato: Worldwide, global.
parole.testo: From French mondial, from Latin mundiālis. Compare Middle English mondiall, mundyall (“worldly, temporal”).

parole.significato: To convert something (especially a security) into currency.
parole.testo: From French monétiser From Latin monēta (whence monnaie) + -iser.

parole.significato: A picture drawn in line only, before the colour and/or shading is applied; an outline sketch.
parole.testo: From French monogramme, from the Classical Latin adjective monogrammus, from the conjectured Ancient Greek * μονόγραμμος (monógrammos, “outlined”, “drawn with single lines”).

parole.significato: A large, single block of stone which is a natural feature; or a block of stone or other similar material used in archit…
parole.testo: The noun is borrowed from French monolithe (“object made from a single block of stone”), from Middle French monolythe (“made from a single block of stone”) (rare), and from their etymon Latin monolithus (“made from a single block of stone”), from Ancient Greek μονόλιθος (monólithos, “made from a sin

parole.significato: The mental and emotional state of a person or group, especially their level of confidence, enthusiasm, and loyalty with…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French morale.

parole.significato: Having or showing a sharp or critical quality.
parole.testo: From French mordant, from Latin mordeō. Doublet of mordent.

parole.significato: Sullen, gloomy; showing a brooding ill humour.
parole.testo: From French morose, from Latin mōrōsus (“particular, scrupulous, fastidious, self-willed, wayward, capricious, fretful, peevish”), from mōs (“way, custom, habit, self-will”). See moral.

parole.significato: The state or quality of being morose.
parole.testo: From French morosité, from Latin morositas (“peevishness”), from morosus (“particular, scrupulous, fastidious, self-willed, wayward, capricious, fretful, peevish”), from mos (“way, custom, habit, self-will”).

parole.significato: A louse.
parole.testo: From French, from mordre (“to bite”) + Latin pedis (“louse”).

parole.significato: A plant of species Adoxa moschatellina, with distinctively configured pale green flowers and a musky smell, of boreal c…
parole.testo: From French moscatelline, from Low Latin moschatellina, from muscus (“musk”).

parole.significato: A light white wine, made from Riesling grapes originating in the valley of this river.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French Moselle, from Latin Mosella.

parole.significato: An old French liquid measure of approximately 274.2 litres.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French muid, from Latin modius. Doublet of modius and mud.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a municipality (a city or a corporation having the right of administering local government).
parole.testo: Borrowed from French municipal, from Latin mūnicipālis (“of or belonging to a citizen or a free town”), from mūniceps (“a citizen, an inhabitant of a free town”), from mūnus (“duty”) + capiō (“to take”).

parole.significato: A district with a government that typically encloses no other governed districts; a borough, city, or incorporated town…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French municipalité (Edmund Burke), from municipal + -ité, from Latin municipalis, from municipium (“free city, township”), from municeps (“citizen of a free city or township”), from mūnus (“duty, service”) + -ceps (“taker, catcher”). Equivalent to municipal + -ity.

parole.significato: A large painting, usually drawn on a wall.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French mural, from Latin muralis, from murus (“wall”).

parole.significato: The common European dormouse.
parole.testo: From French muscadin (“a musk-scented lozenge”), from muscade (“nutmeg”), from Latin muscus (“musk”), so called from its odour. See muscadel.

parole.significato: The inability to speak, be it from psychological or physical cause.
parole.testo: From French mutisme, from Latin mutus (“mute”), equivalent to mute + -ism.

parole.significato: An aura of heightened interest, meaning or mystery surrounding a person or thing.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French mystique (“a mystic”), from Latin mysticus. See also the doublet mystic.

parole.significato: Legal membership of a particular nation or state, by origin, birth, naturalization, ownership, allegiance or otherwise.
parole.testo: From national + -ity, perhaps after French nationalité; ultimately from Latin nātio (“nation, people”).

parole.significato: shipwreck
parole.testo: From French naufrage (“shipwreck”), from Latin naufragium (“shipwreck”), from nāvis (“ship”) + frangere (“to break”).

parole.significato: Someone who conducts negotiations; a negotiator, an agent.
parole.testo: From French négociant, or its source, Latin negōtiant-, probably via Italian negoziante (“merchant”).

parole.significato: Chiefly of a person: having a neutral gender (being neither male nor female), and having or seeking to have no or reduc…
parole.testo: Apparently a blend of French neu(tre) (“neuter”, adjective) or its etymon Latin neu(ter) (“neuter”, adjective) + French trois (“three”) (referring to the third gender), coined by Holly A. Burnham in 1995 as a self-description.

parole.significato: A work in a genre of piano music of moderate tempo with a highly-decorated, improvisatory melody.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French nocturne (literally “nocturnal”), from Latin nocturnus. Doublet of notturno.

parole.significato: Capable of being identified using a name.
parole.testo: From French nominable or its etymon Latin nōminābilis, from nōminō (“to name”) + -ābilis (“-able”).

parole.significato: Casually calm and relaxed.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French nonchalant, from Old French nonchaloir (“to be unconcerned”), from non- (“not”) + chaloir (“to have concern for”), from Latin non (“not”) + calēre (“to be warm”).

parole.significato: Knotted; tied in a knot.
parole.testo: From French noué, past participle of nouer (“to knot”), from Latin nodare. See nodated.

parole.significato: A minor distinction.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French nuance (“nuance, shade, hue”). Omitting several steps, from Latin nūbēs. Compare typologically Italian sfumatura (< Latin fūmus).

parole.significato: Of an age suitable for marriage; marriageable (principally of a young woman).
parole.testo: From French nubile, from Latin nūbilis (“marriageable”), from nūbō (“marry, to take as husband”), from Proto-Indo-European *snewbʰ- (“to marry, to wed”). Possibly cognate with Ancient Greek νύμφη (númphē, “bride, young wife, nymph”) (English nymph), but this is disputed.

parole.significato: The tissue which surrounds and protects the embryo and lies inside of the integuments.
parole.testo: From French nucelle (“little nut”), from Latin nux (“nut”).

parole.significato: A nulligravid person.
parole.testo: Borrowed from terms in Romance languages such as French nulligeste, from Latin nūllus (“none”) + gestus (“borne, carried”).

parole.significato: A protozoan from the Tertiary period, known only as fossils.
parole.testo: From French nummulite, and its source, Latin nummulus (“little coin”); and from scientific Latin Nummulites (genus name). By surface analysis, numm(us) + -ule + -ite.

parole.significato: Used when giving the former name of a man.
parole.testo: From French né, from Old French né, from Latin nātus, perfect active participle of nāscor (“to be born”). Doublet of nada.

parole.significato: Carelessly or unceremoniously dressed.
parole.testo: From French négligée f (past participle, adjective), from French négligé m (“underdressed; loose garment”, past participle, adjective, noun), past participle of négliger (“to neglect”), from Latin negligere.

parole.significato: The state of being obese.
parole.testo: From French obésité, from Latin obēsitās, from obēsus (“fat”). By surface analysis, obese + -ity.

parole.significato: An eye doctor; an ophthalmologist or optometrist.
parole.testo: From French oculiste (“oculist”), from Latin oculus (“eye”).

parole.significato: A work of art, music or literature.
parole.testo: From French œuvre, from Old French uevre, from Latin opera (plural of Latin opus), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ep- (“work”). Doublet of opera, opus, and ure.

parole.significato: The charge, office, court, or jurisdiction of an official.
parole.testo: From official + -ity; or French officialité, from Latin officialitas.

parole.significato: Medicinal.
parole.testo: From French, from Latin officīna (“a workshop”), contracted from opificīna, from opifex (“a workman”); opus (“work”) + faciō (“to make or do”).

parole.significato: A large, grotesque, brutish humanoid monster, typically marked by great strength and a propensity to kill or devour hum…
parole.testo: First attested in the 18th century, borrowed from French ogre, from Latin Orcus (“god of the underworld”), from Ancient Greek Ὅρκος (Hórkos), the personified demon of oaths (ὅρκος (hórkos, “oath”)) who inflicts punishment upon oath-breakers. Doublet of orc and Orcus.

parole.significato: A round hole or circle with which an opening for an arrowslit terminates.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French œillet, from œil (“eye”), from Latin oculum, accusative singular of oculus.

parole.significato: A bus (vehicle for transporting large numbers of people along roads).
parole.testo: Borrowed from French (voiture) omnibus (“(carriage) for all”), from Latin omnibus (“for all”), dative plural of omnis (“all”).

parole.significato: An oogonium.
parole.testo: Attested in English since 1863. From French oogone (“oogonium”) or directly from its source, scientific Latin oogonium, from Ancient Greek ᾠόν (ōión) egg + Ancient Greek γόνος (gónos) begetting.

parole.significato: The state or quality of being opaque, not allowing light to pass through.
parole.testo: From opaque + -ity, from French opacité, from Latin opācitās, from opācus.

parole.significato: A mineral consisting, like quartz, of silica, but inferior to quartz in hardness and specific gravity, of the chemical…
parole.testo: In Florio’s A World of Words 1598 as opale, from French opale, from Latin opalus, from Byzantine Greek ὀπάλλιος (opállios), from Sanskrit उपल (upala, “gem, stone”), from उपरि (upári, “the upper millstone”). Distantly related to over.

parole.significato: To choose; select.
parole.testo: First attested in 1853; borrowed from French opter, from Latin optō (“to choose; to select”). Doublet of optate.

parole.significato: One of a set of choices that can be made.
parole.testo: From French option, from Latin optiō (“choice; option; act of choosing”), from optō (“to choose, select”). Equivalent to opt + -ion.

parole.significato: Wealth.
parole.testo: From French opulence, from Latin opulentia.

parole.significato: Wine for ordinary use.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French ordinaire.

parole.significato: A sweet syrup made from sugar and almonds (or originally barley) and rose water or orange-flower water.
parole.testo: From French orgeat, derived from orge (“barley”), from Latin hordeum. Doublet of horchata and orzo. Cognate to Surinamese Dutch orgeade.

parole.significato: Any of a number of long, thick pieces of timber, pointed and shod with iron, and suspended, each by a separate rope, ov…
parole.testo: From French orgue, from Latin organum (“organ, instrument, tool”), from Ancient Greek ὄργανον (órganon, “organ, instrument, tool”). Doublet of organ, organon, and organum.

parole.significato: A secret rite or ceremony, typically involving riotous and dissolute behavior, including dancing, drunkenness and indis…
parole.testo: Originally in plural from French orgies, from Latin orgia, from Ancient Greek ὄργια (órgia, “secret rites, mysteries”).

parole.significato: A semicircular or squared off projection made at the shoulder of a bastion for the purpose of covering the retired flan…
parole.testo: From French orillon (literally “little ear”), from oreille (“an ear”), from Latin oricula, auricula, diminutive of auris (“an ear”). See ear.

parole.significato: A cloth made of worsted and cotton, used for making clothes.
parole.testo: From French Orléans, ultimately from Latin Aurelianum, from the name of the Roman emperor Aurelian, who rebuilt the city. More at Aurelius.

parole.significato: the act of oscillating or the state of being oscillated
parole.testo: From French oscillation, from Latin oscillatio, from Latin oscillo. By surface analysis, oscillate + -ion.

parole.significato: A skeletal framework; an underlying structure.
parole.testo: From French ossature, from Latin os (“bone”) + -ature.

parole.significato: To transform (or cause to transform) from a softer animal substance into bone; particularly the processes of growth in…
parole.testo: Back-formation from ossification, or modeled on French ossifier and formed from Latin os, ossis (“bone”) + -ify.

parole.significato: Apparent, evident; meant for open display.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French ostensible, formed with the suffix -ible, from Latin ostensus, the past participle of ostendō (“show”), itself from obs- (“in front of”) (akin to ob- (“in the way”)) + tendō (“stretch”) (akin to Ancient Greek τείνω (teínō)). Cf. ostentatious.

parole.significato: The structure in a plant that develops into a seed after fertilization; the megasporangium of a seed plant with its enc…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French ovule (“ovum”), from Latin ōvum (“egg”). Doublet of ovolo.

parole.significato: Of or relating to a palace.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French palatial, formed from the root of Latin palātium (“a palace”), from Palātium (“Palatine Hill”).

parole.significato: A thin mattress or under bed stuffed with straw.
parole.testo: French French paillasse, from Old French paille (“straw, chaff”), from Latin palea (“chaff”).

parole.significato: One of the most common saturated fatty acids; it is found in all animal and most vegetable oils and fats; it is used in…
parole.testo: From being an acid discovered in saponified palm oils. From French palmite (“pith of the palm tree”) + -ic. From Latin palma (“palm tree”).

parole.significato: An ornament, composed of vine leaves and bunches of grapes, used for decorating spiral columns.
parole.testo: From French pampre (“a vine branch”), from Latin pampinus.

parole.significato: A small dog of a certain toy spaniel breed having large upright ears with a shape that resembles butterfly wings.
parole.testo: From French papillon (“butterfly”), from Latin pāpiliō (“butterfly, moth”). Doublet of papilio and pavilion.

parole.significato: A kind of parchment made by soaking unsized paper in dilute sulphuric acid.
parole.testo: From French papyrine, from Latin papȳrus + French -ine.

parole.significato: By; with.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French par (“through, by”), from Latin per (“through”). Doublet of per.

parole.significato: Because or on account of one's excellence.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French par excellence (“excellently, in an especially representative way; above all”), a calque of Latin per excellentiam, itself a calque of Ancient Greek κατ’ ἐξοχήν (kat’ exokhḗn).

parole.significato: Someone suffering from paralysis.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French paralytique, from Latin paralyticus, from Ancient Greek παραλυτικός (paralutikós, “paralyzed”).

parole.significato: A person who has risen, climbed up, or has been promoted to a higher social class, especially through acquisition of we…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French parvenu, past participle of parvenir, from Latin perveniō (“arrive, reach”). See also parvenue f

parole.significato: Synonym of pedagogical.
parole.testo: First attested in 1781. From French pédagogique, from Latin paedagōgicus, pēdagōgicus, from Ancient Greek παιδαγωγικός (paidagōgikós), from παιδαγωγός (paidagōgós, “teacher, tutor”), from παῖς (paîs, “child”) + ἄγω (ágō, “to lead”).

parole.significato: The duty on hides, furs and skins.
parole.testo: From French pellage, from Latin pellicula, from pellis (“a skin”). By surface analysis, pell + -age.

parole.significato: A group of riders formed during a cycling road race; especially, the main group of riders; the pack.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French peloton (“small ball (of thread, etc.), pellet; (cycling) group of riders formed during a cycling road race; (military) small group of soldiers, platoon”), from pelote (“small ball (of thread, etc.)”) (ultimately from Latin pila (“ball; ball game; globe, sphere”) (probably refer

parole.significato: A drop-shaped diamond or other gem used as a pendant; also, a piece of jewellery in pendant form.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French pendeloque (“hanging object; religious medallion, probably in pendant form; jewel hanging from an earring; small crystal piece, especially one hanging from a chandelier”) [and other forms], from Old French pendeloche (“penis”) (apparently a hapax legomenon), from pendeler (“to d

parole.significato: A genre of Italian films based on historical or biblical epics.
parole.testo: From French péplum, from Latin peplum, from Ancient Greek πέπλων (péplōn), neuter of πέπλος (péplos).

parole.significato: The point, in an orbit about the Earth, that is closest to the Earth: the periapsis of an Earth orbiter.
parole.testo: From French périgée via Latin perigeum, perigaeum, ultimately from Ancient Greek περί (perí, “near”) + γῆ (gê, “Earth”).

parole.significato: A colonnade surrounding a courtyard, temple, etc., or the yard enclosed by such columns.
parole.testo: From French péristyle, from Classical Latin peristȳlum, from Ancient Greek περίστυλον (perístulon), from περι- (peri-, “around”) + στῦλος (stûlos, “pillar”), equivalent to peri- + -style.

parole.significato: Good-natured banter; raillery.
parole.testo: From French persiflage, from persifler (“to quiz, tease, mock”), from per- + siffler (“to whistle”), from Latin sībilō (“whistle”).

parole.significato: The act of persuading, or trying to do so; the addressing of arguments to someone with the intention of changing their…
parole.testo: From French persuasion and its source, Latin persuāsiō, from persuādēre, from suādēre (“to advise, recommend”).

parole.significato: A text describing medicines and pharmacological substances, especially their use, preparation, and regulation.
parole.testo: From French pharmacopée and post-classical Latin pharmacopoeia, from Hellenistic Ancient Greek φαρμακοποιία (pharmakopoiía, “preparation of drugs”).

parole.significato: A branch of biology that deals with the functions and activities of life or of living matter (as organs, tissues, or ce…
parole.testo: From French physiologie, from Latin physiologia, from Ancient Greek φυσιολογία (phusiología, “natural philosophy”), from φύσις (phúsis, “nature”) + λόγος (lógos, “word”). Equivalent to physio- + -logy.

parole.significato: Requiring atonement or reparation: wicked, sinful, bad.
parole.testo: Early 17th century, from French piaculaire, from Latin piacularis, derived from piaculum, from piō (“to appease, purify, expiate”) +-culum (instrumental suffix).

parole.significato: To make a raid for booty; to maraud or loot.
parole.testo: From French picorer (“to go marauding, originally to steal cattle”), ultimately from Latin pecoris (“cattle”).

parole.significato: In the shape of a pine cone.
parole.testo: From French pinéal, from Middle French, from Latin pīnea (“pine cone, pine nut”), from pīneus (“of the pine”).

parole.significato: calm and quiet; peaceful; tranquil
parole.testo: Borrowed from French placide, from Latin placidus (“peaceful, calm, placid”), from placeō (“please, satisfy”).

parole.significato: Synonym of plainsong.
parole.testo: From French plain-chant, from plain + chant, calque of Latin cantus planus.

parole.significato: Of an animal: walking with the entire sole of the foot on the ground.
parole.testo: From French plantigrade, from Latin planta (“sole of the foot”) (from Proto-Indo-European *pléh₂-n̥t-eh₂, from *pleh₂- (“flat”)) + -grade, from Latin gradus (“pace, step”).

parole.significato: The embryo which has begun its development in the act of germination; a seedling.
parole.testo: From French plantule, diminutive of plante (“a plant”), Latin planta.

parole.significato: A direct popular vote on an issue of public importance, such as an amendment to the constitution, a change in the sover…
parole.testo: Sense 1 (“referendum”) is borrowed from French plébiscite, from Latin plēbiscītum, plēbis scītum, plēbī scītum (“law of the common people or plebs”), from plēbis (the genitive singular of plēbs (“common people, plebeians”)) + scītum (“decree, ordinance, statute”). parole.significato: A block or slab upon which a column, pedestal, statue or other structure is based.
parole.testo: From French plinthe, from Latin plinthus, from Ancient Greek πλίνθος (plínthos, “brick”).

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or produced by rain.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French pluvial, from Middle French pluvial, borrowed from Latin pluviālis (“pertaining to rain”).

parole.significato: A politician, especially one seen as being unprincipled.
parole.testo: From French politique, from Latin politicus. Doublet of politic.

parole.significato: A roundel vert (green circular spot), resembling or representing an apple.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French pomme (“apple”), ultimately from Latin poma. Doublet of pome.

parole.significato: The deliberate slaughter of a people or a nation.
parole.testo: Probably an unadapted borrowing from French populicide (“(noun) slaughter of a people; (adjective) harmful to the people”) (obsolete, rare), from Latin populus (“community; people; nation”) + French -cide (suffix meaning ‘killing’). parole.significato: A gateway through which horse carriages pass, often into a courtyard.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French porte cochère (literally “coach gateway or coachman's gateway”): porte (“door; gateway”) (ultimately from Latin porta (“door; entrance; gate; passage”), from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“to go through; to carry forth, fare”)) + cochère (from coche (“stagecoach”) + -ièr

parole.significato: A girl, a young woman, especially seen as promiscuous; a slut.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French poule, from Latin pullus, pulla.

parole.significato: A type of fine powder, as of sandarac, or cuttlefish bone, sprinkled over wet ink to dry the ink after writing or on ro…
parole.testo: From French ponce, from Latin pūmex. Doublet of pumice.

parole.significato: Previous caution or care; caution previously employed to prevent misfortune or to secure good.
parole.testo: From French précaution, Latin praecautio, from praecavere, praecautum (“to guard against beforehand”); prae (“before”) + cavere (“be on one's guard”). See pre-, and caution.

parole.significato: The person who leads songs or prayers in a cathedral, church, monastery, or synagogue and generally facilitates worship.
parole.testo: From French précenteur, from Latin praecentor, from praecentus (“sung before”), from praecinō (“to sing before”) + -or (“agent suffix”), from prae- + canĕre (“to sing”).

parole.significato: Able to take hold of and clasp objects; adapted for grasping especially by wrapping around an object.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French préhensile, from Latin perfect passive participle prehēnsus, from prehendō (“grasp, seize”) + adjective suffix -ile, from Latin -ilis.

parole.significato: prelates in general
parole.testo: From both French prélature and post-Classical Latin praelātūra.

parole.significato: The power or right of taking a thing before it is offered
parole.testo: Borrowed from French prendre (“to take”), from Latin prehendere (“to take”).

parole.significato: The quality of how good the reputation of something or someone is, how favourably something or someone is regarded.
parole.testo: From French prestige (“illusion, fascination, enchantment, prestige”), from Latin praestīgium (“a delusion, an illusion”). Despite the phonetic similarities and the old meaning of “delusion, illusion, trick”, the word has a different root than prestidigitator (“conjurer”) and prestidigitation.

parole.significato: Motivated by an inappropriate, excessive, or unjustified desire to impress others.
parole.testo: From French prétentieux, from prétention, from Latin praetēnsus (“false or hypocritical profession”), past participle of praetendō. parole.significato: To precede (come before) or anticipate.
parole.testo: From French prévenir, Latin praevenire. See prevent.

parole.significato: A mammal of the order Primates, comprising of apes (including humans), monkeys, lemurs, tarsiers, lorisids, and galagos.
parole.testo: First attested in 1876. From French primate, from the substantivization of Latin prīmās, prīmātis (“one of the first, chief, excellent, noble”), same as Etymology 2. So named due to the belief that primates are the highest order of mammals or animals.

parole.significato: Synonym of prize.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French prix, from Old French pris. Compare English price.

parole.significato: A particular method for performing a task.
parole.testo: From French procédure, from Old French, from Latin procedere (“to go forward, proceed”); see proceed.

parole.significato: Synonym of proletarian.
parole.testo: * From French prolétaire, from Latin prōlētārius.

parole.significato: The lowest class of society; also, the lower classes of society generally; the masses.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French prolétariat, from prolétaire + -at, from Latin proletārius, from prōlēt- (“offspring”) + -ārius, from stem of prōlēs, from pro- + *olēs (“growth”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂el- (“to grow, nourish”). By surface analysis, Latin prōlēt- + -ary + -at.

parole.significato: Fertile; producing offspring or fruit in abundance, applied to plants producing fruit, animals producing young, etc.
parole.testo: First use appears c. 1635. From French prolifique and its etymon Latin prōlificus, from prōlēs (“offspring”) + -ficus (“making”).

parole.significato: The state of being prominent: widely known or eminent.
parole.testo: From obsolete French prominence (compare proéminence), from Latin prominentia.

parole.significato: Standing out, or projecting; jutting; protuberant.
parole.testo: From obsolete French prominent (compare proéminent), from Latin prōminēns, present active participle of prōmineō (“jut out, to project”), from prō (“before, forward”) + mineō (in compounds, “jut, project”).

parole.significato: Walking on the inner edge of the foot.
parole.testo: From French pronation, from Latin pronatio.

parole.significato: Propensity.
parole.testo: From French propension, and its source, Latin prōpēnsiō, from the participle stem of prōpendeō.

parole.significato: Of or relating to property or ownership.
parole.testo: From French propriétaire, from Latin proprietārius. By surface analysis, propriety + -ary. Compare with the Latin proprietas (“property”) and proprius (“ownership”).

parole.significato: A document, distributed to prospective members, investors, buyers, or participants, which describes an institution (suc…
parole.testo: From French prospectus (“a prospectus”), borrowed from Latin prospectus. Doublet of prospect and prospekt.

parole.significato: A bulge, knob, swelling, spine, or anything that protrudes.
parole.testo: From French protubérance, from Latin prōtubērantia (“bulge; protuberance”), from prō + tūber (“swelling; protuberance”) + -antia (“-ance”).

parole.significato: A person who is guided and supported by an older and more experienced person (a protector or mentor).
parole.testo: Borrowed from French protégé, past participle of protéger (“to protect”).

parole.significato: Place or source of origin.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French provenance (“origin”), from Middle French provenant, present participle of provenir (“come forth, arise”), from Latin provenio (“to come forth”).

parole.significato: To lay a stock or branch of a vine in the ground for propagation.
parole.testo: From French provigner, from provin (“a set, layer of a plant”), Old French provain, from Latin propago, propaginis, akin to propagare (“to propagate”). See propagate and prune.

parole.significato: A person who is or tries to be excessively proper, especially one who is easily offended by matters of a sexual nature.
parole.testo: From French prude, from Old French prude, prode, feminine of prou, prod, prud (“good, excellent, brave”), from Latin prōde. Related to proud but unrelated to prudent.

parole.significato: A brownish-purple color, sometimes more or less deep red or grayish.
parole.testo: From French couleur puce, from Latin pūlex (“flea”).

parole.significato: A sense of modesty, shame, or reserve, especially as relating to sexual matters.
parole.testo: From French pudeur, from Latin pudor. Doublet of pudor.

parole.significato: Easily ashamed, having a strong sense of shame; modest, chaste.
parole.testo: From French pudique, from Latin pudīcus, from pudet (“it shames”).

parole.significato: The act of driving forward; propulsion.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French pulsion, from Latin pulsio.

parole.significato: A bedbug.
parole.testo: From French punaise, from punais (“stinking”), from Latin putere.

parole.significato: Something undergoing, or having undergone putrefaction.
parole.testo: French putrilage, Latin putrilago (“putrefaction”).

parole.significato: A priest of the Roman Catholic Church, especially a French one. Also used as a title preceding the name of such a pries…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French père (“father”), from Latin pater. Doublet of ayr, faeder, father, padre, and pater.

parole.significato: Square-shaped.
parole.testo: From French quadratique (1765), from Latin quadrātus + -ique (English -ic), form of quadrō (“to make square”), from quādrus (“square”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kʷetwóres (“four”), whence also Latin quartus (“fourth”).

parole.significato: A four-footed or four-legged animal.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French quadrupède, from Middle French, from Latin stem of quadrupēs (“four-footed, a four-footed animal”), from quadri- (“four-”) + stem of pes (“foot”). Alternatively analyzable as quadru- + -ped. Doublet of tetrapod.

parole.significato: With little or no sound; free of disturbing noise.
parole.testo: From Middle English quiete, from Old French quiet (adjective) and quiete (noun), from Latin quiētus, past participle of quiēscere (“to keep quiet, rest”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kʷyeh₁- (“rest”). parole.significato: a stew of meat and vegetables mixed together
parole.testo: Borrowed from French ragoût. Compare ragù of the same origin, borrowed from Italian.

parole.significato: A softening or mollifying; softness
parole.testo: From French ramollir (“to make soft, to soften”), from re- (“re-”) + amollir (“to soften”), from a (Latin ad) + mollir (“to soften”), from Latin mollire, from mollis (“soft”).

parole.significato: speed, swiftness; the condition of being rapid
parole.testo: From rapid + -ity, from French rapidité, from Latin rapiditas.

parole.significato: A liqueur or cordial flavored with peach or cherry kernels, bitter almonds, or other fruits.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Creole French ratafia, from the Latin phrase rata fiat (conventio) (“the deal is made”), a drinking toast expression to celebrate a deal or an agreement. Or, sharing an Arabic origin with arak.

parole.significato: Reasoning, conscious deliberate inference; the activity or process of reasoning.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French ratiocination, from Latin ratiōcinātiō (“argumentation, reasoning, ratiocination; a syllogism”), from ratiōcinātus (“reckoned”) + -tiō (suffix forming a noun relating to some action or the result of an action). parole.significato: A thick, coarse, woolen twill.
parole.testo: From French ratine, from Old French rastin, from Latin raster (“to scrape”), ultimately from Latin rādere (“rash”).

parole.significato: To devastate, destroy or lay waste to something.
parole.testo: From French ravage (“ravage, havoc, spoil”), from ravir (“to bear away suddenly”), from Latin rapere (“to snatch, seize”), akin to Ancient Greek ἁρπάζω (harpázō, “to seize”).

parole.significato: A deep narrow valley or gorge in the earth's surface worn by running water.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French ravin (“a gully”), from Old French raviner (“to pillage, sweep down, cascade”), from ravine (“robbery, rapine; violent rush of water, waterfall, avalanche; impetuosity, spirit”), from Latin rapīna (cf. rapine).
