parole.significato: Irritating, repellent.
parole.testo: From French rébarbatif, rébarbative (“repellent, disagreeable”), from Middle French rebarber (“to oppose”), ultimately from Latin barba (“beard”), literally “to stand beard to beard against”.

parole.significato: Marked by a stubborn unwillingness to obey authority.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French récalcitrant, in derived from Latin recalcitrāns, recalcitrantis, present participle of recalcitrō, recalcitrāre (“be disobedient, kick back [as a horse]”), from calx (“heel”), 1820s.

parole.significato: Committing new offenses after a crime committed in the past.
parole.testo: From French récidivisme, from Latin recidīvus (“returning, recurring”). Compare recidivous, -ism. By surface analysis, recidive + -ism.

parole.significato: One who falls back into prior habits, especially criminal habits.
parole.testo: From French récidiviste, from Latin recidīvus (“returning, recurring”). Compare recidivous, -ist. By surface analysis, recidive + -ist.

parole.significato: The act of recollecting, or recalling to the memory; the act of recalling to memory.
parole.testo: Via French récollection or the verb recollect, both from Latin recollectus, the past participle of recolligere (“to collect again”), itself from re- + colligere (“to gather”).

parole.significato: To perform a reconnaissance (of an area; an enemy position); to scout with the aim of acquiring information.
parole.testo: From French reconnoître (obsolete spelling of reconnaître), from Latin recognoscere (“to recognize”). Contrarily, there is also an obsolete 19th-century British English spelling reconnaitre (now reconnoitre).

parole.significato: To perform a reconnaissance (of an area; an enemy position); to scout with the aim of gaining information.
parole.testo: From French reconnoître (obsolete spelling of reconnaître), from Latin recognoscere (“to recognise”). There is also an obsolete 19th-century British English spelling reconnaitre, influenced by the modern French form.

parole.significato: Mental or spiritual refreshment.
parole.testo: From French réfection, from Latin refectiōnem, accusative singular of refectiō (“recovery, refection”), from reficiō (“restore, renew”).

parole.significato: A reformer.
parole.testo: Partly borrowed from French réformateur and partly directly from Latin reformātor.

parole.significato: The chorus or burden of a song repeated at the end of each verse or stanza.
parole.testo: From French refrain, from the Old French verb refraindre (“to break off, repeat”), from Latin re- (“back, again”) + frangō (“break”); compare Occitan refranhs (“a refrain”), refranher (“to repeat”). See refract and the verb refrain.

parole.significato: A person seeking refuge (as for shelter or protection), especially in a foreign country, out of fear or prospect of pol…
parole.testo: From French réfugié, past participle of réfugier (“to take refuge, to seek refuge”), from Old French refuge (“hiding place”) from Latin refugium (“a place of refuge, place to flee back to”), originally describing French Huguenots fleeing religious persecution after the revocation of the Edict of Nan

parole.significato: regulation
parole.testo: From French réglement, from régler, from Latin regulare. See regulate.

parole.significato: The act of rejecting.
parole.testo: From French réjection or directly from Latin reiectiōnem, accusative of Latin reiectiō. Displaced native Old English āworpennes (literally “thrown-out-ness”).

parole.significato: Recall by means of the memory; remembrance.
parole.testo: French remémoration, or Latin rememoratio.

parole.significato: Any of several small, marine, cave-dwelling crustaceans, of the class Remipedia, characterized by a short head and a lo…
parole.testo: From French rémipède, partly modelled on Latin.

parole.significato: To sew together so that the seam is scarcely visible; to sew up with skill and nicety; to finedraw.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French rentraire; Latin prefix re- (“re-”) + in (“into, in”) + trahere (“to draw”).

parole.significato: Synonym of findable: able to be found.
parole.testo: From French repertible, from Latin repertus (“found, discovered, invented”), from reperīre (“to find, discover, invent”), from re- (“again, anew”) + parere (“to bear, to get”), + French -ible (“-able”). Cognate with repertitious, repertor, reperible.

parole.significato: A metalworking technique in which a malleable metal is ornamented or shaped by hammering from the reverse side.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French repoussé (“pushed up”), ultimately from Latin pulsare (“to push”).

parole.significato: The act of reprobating; the state of being reprobated; strong disapproval, reproof or censure.
parole.testo: From French réprobation, or Latin reprobatio. By surface analysis, reprobate + -ion.

parole.significato: Any of various plants of the genus Reseda having small, pale grayish green flowers, such as dyer's rocket (Reseda luteo…
parole.testo: From French réséda, from Latin resēda, said by Pliny the Elder (23–79 C.E.) to be from resēdāre (“to soothe”), from re- (“again”) + sēdāre (“to assuage, calm”)), an allusion to the healing properties of the plant.

parole.significato: Resounding, echoing.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French résonnant or Latin resonantem.

parole.significato: An eating establishment in which diners are served food, usually by waiters at their tables but sometimes (as in a fast…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French restaurant, present participle of the verb restaurer, corresponding to Latin restaurans, restaurantis, present participle of restauro (“to restore”), from the name of the 'restorative' soup served in the first establishments.

parole.significato: A summary or synopsis.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French résumé, past participle of résumer (“to summarize”), from Latin resūmere (“to take back”); compare resume.

parole.significato: A reticle; a grid in the eyepiece of an instrument.
parole.testo: From French réticule, from Latin rēticulum, diminutive of rēte (“net”). Doublet of reticle, reticulum, and Reticulum.

parole.significato: Of, or relating to, the past, past times, or the way things were.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French rétro, ultimately from Latin retro.

parole.significato: To regard someone or something with great awe or devotion.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French révérer, ultimately from Latin revereor, from re- + vereor (“to fear”).

parole.significato: Having reverted to a previous (more basic or more natural) state.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French revertent, from Latin revertor, equivalent to revert + -ent.

parole.significato: The process of revising:
parole.testo: Borrowed from French révision, from Latin revīsiō.

parole.significato: To reanimate, bring back to life.
parole.testo: Partly from French revivifier and partly from Latin revīvificō, corresponding to re- + vivify.

parole.significato: Broken, as an ordinary; cut off, or broken at the top, as a chevron, a bend, etc.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French rompu, past participle of rompre to break, Latin rumpō. See rupture.

parole.significato: A heavyweight breed of domesticated duck, of French origin.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French Rouen, from Latin Rotomagus. Replaced Middle English Rone, from Anglo-Norman Ron.

parole.significato: Of a reddish pink colour.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French rouge, from Latin rubeus. Compare rare Middle English rouge, rouȝ (“red”); later borrowed again, as it is not attested until c. 1750. The game senses are of unknown origin according to the Oxford English Dictionary.

parole.significato: cabling
parole.testo: From French rudenture, from Latin rudens (“rope”).

parole.significato: Any of many box-, tube- or ring-shaped marine heterodont bivalves from the Jurassic and Cretaceous periods.
parole.testo: From French rudistes (plural), from rude (“rough, uneven”), or its source, Latin rudis. Compare scientific Latin Rudista.

parole.significato: A bag or pouch inside a plant or animal that typically contains a fluid.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French sac. Doublet of saccus, sack, saco, and sakkos.

parole.significato: The quality of being sage, wise, or able to make good decisions; the quality of being perceptive, astute or insightful.
parole.testo: From French sagacité, from Latin sagācitās (“sagaciousness”), from sagāx (“of quick perception, acute, sagacious”) (whence -acity), from sāgiō (“to perceive by the senses”). Equivalent to sagac(ious) + -ity.

parole.significato: acicular rutile occurring in reticulated forms embedded in quartz
parole.testo: From French sagénite, from Latin sagena (“a large net”). See saine.

parole.significato: To react so as to form a salt
parole.testo: From French salifier; from Latin sal (“salt”) + -ficare (“to make”) (only in comparative). See -fy.

parole.significato: A sortie of troops from a besieged place against an enemy.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French saillie, from sailli, the past participle of the verb saillir (“to leap forth”), itself from Latin salīre (“to leap”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to health.
parole.testo: 19th century, borrowed from French sanitaire, formed from Latin sanitas (“health”). Analysable as sanity + -ary.

parole.significato: A soapy mixture obtained by treating an essential oil with an alkali; hence, any similar compound of an essential oil.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French saponule, from Latin sapo (“soap”) + -onis.

parole.significato: Any one of several species of small herring which are commonly preserved in olive oil or in tins for food, especially t…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French sardine (cognate with Spanish sardina, Italian sardina), Latin sardīna; from Ancient Greek σαρδίνη (sardínē).

parole.significato: A chassé.
parole.testo: Verlan (or metathesis) form of French chassé, past participle of chasser (“chase”), from Latin captō, frequentative of capiō (“to take”).

parole.significato: A sylvan deity or demigod, male companion of Pan or Dionysus, represented as part man and part goat, and characterized…
parole.testo: From French satyre, from Latin satyrus, from Ancient Greek σάτυρος (sáturos).

parole.significato: A person of learning, especially one who is versed in literature or science.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French savant, from Latin sapiō. Doublet of sapient. Sense 3 is a clipping of idiot savant, literally ‘wise idiot’.

parole.significato: A criminal, a villain.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French scélérat, from Latin scelerātus, past participle of scelerāre (“to pollute, defile”), from scelus (“crime”).

parole.significato: Any of a variety of coarse-grained crystalline metamorphic rocks with a foliated structure that allows easy division in…
parole.testo: From French schiste, from Latin schistos lapis (“the stone that is easy to split”), from Ancient Greek σχιστός (skhistós, “splittable”), from σχίζω (skhízō, “to split”).

parole.significato: Metal scraps or clippings; especially the remains of fillets from which coin blanks have been cut.
parole.testo: From French cisailles (“scissels”), from cisailler (“to clip with shears”), from cisailles (“scissors”), from Latin caesaculum, from caesus, from caedere (“to cut, hew”).

parole.significato: To form by sculpture.
parole.testo: From French sculpter, from Latin sculpō (“to cut out, carve in stone”).

parole.significato: Scurrilous.
parole.testo: From French scurrile, from Latin scurrilis.

parole.significato: Any substance that is secreted by an organism.
parole.testo: (1646) From French sécrétion, from Latin sēcrētiō, sēcrētiōnem.

parole.significato: A seat or stool.
parole.testo: From French selle, from Latin sella.

parole.significato: Of, or relating to old age.

parole.significato: An electric motor in a servomechanism, especially one which incorporates feedback so it accurately positions the device.

parole.significato: To hammer and squeeze material in order to expel cinder and impurities from it, as in metallurgy.

parole.significato: A sibilant rale.

parole.significato: A long dry fruit (seed capsule), length more than twice the width, typical to cruciferous plants and consisting of two…
parole.testo: From French silique, from Latin siliqua (“a pod or husk, a very small weight or measure”). Doublet of siliqua.

parole.significato: An alloy of copper and zinc, resembling brass, but of a golden color.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a grammatical form or construction that expresses the individuation of a single referent from a mas…

parole.significato: sinopia (clay)
parole.testo: From French [Term?], from Latin sinopis (terra) (“a red earth or ocher found in Sinope”), from Sinope (“a town in Paphlagoma, on the Black Sea”).

parole.significato: The character of being social; sociability
parole.testo: From social + -ity, from French socialité or directly from Latin sociālitās (“fellowship, sociality”), from sociālis (“social”), from socius (“companion, ally”) + -ālis.

parole.testo: From French sociologie, coined by Auguste Comte in 1834, itself a combination of Latin socius (“companion, fellowship”) and the Greek suffix Ancient Greek -λογία (-logía), itself from Ancient Greek λόγος (lógos, “word, knowledge”), from socio- + -logy. parole.significato: A fraternity, a society or association.

parole.significato: Living or being alone; solitary.

parole.significato: A fluid that dissolves a solid, liquid, or gaseous solute, resulting in a solution.

parole.significato: Dark; gloomy; shadowy, dimly lit.

parole.significato: Pertaining to dreams.
parole.testo: From obsolete French somnial, from Latin somnialis, from somnium (“dream”).

parole.significato: Drowsy or sleepy.

parole.significato: The property of being sonorous.
parole.testo: From sonor(ous) + -ity, from French sonorité, from Latin sonōritās.

parole.significato: Something inducing sleep, especially a drug.
parole.testo: From French soporifique, from Latin sopor (“deep sleep”). Unrelated to stupor (distinct in Proto-Indo-European).

parole.significato: A sou (the French coin).

parole.significato: An item of sentimental value, that is given or kept to remember an event or location.

parole.significato: Silk.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French soie (“silk”), soye, from Middle French soye, from Old French soie, earlier seie, from Latin sēta, saeta, from Proto-Italic *saitā, from Proto-Indo-European *séh₂ito-, *sh₂éyto-, from *sh₂ey-, *seh₂i- (“to bind”). Doublet of seta.

parole.significato: Any of several hard minerals of cubic symmetry that are mixed oxides of magnesium and aluminium and are used as gemston…
parole.testo: French spinelle, perhaps from Latin spina (“a thorn, a prickle”), in allusion to its pointed crystals.

parole.significato: Synonym of haustellum (“sucking organ”).

parole.significato: A small spore
parole.testo: From French sporule or Latin sporula; equivalent to spore + -ule.

parole.significato: A European bulbous liliaceous plant, of the genus Scilla, used in medicine for its acrid, expectorant, diuretic, and em…
parole.testo: From French scille, from Latin scilla. Doublet of scilla.

parole.significato: Lacking flow or motion, and thus usually not fresh or healthy; decaying through stillness.

parole.significato: The stem of a mushroom, kelp, etc.
parole.testo: From French stipe, from Latin stīpes (“a stock, post, branch”).

parole.significato: A basal appendage of a typical leaf of a flowering plant, usually appearing paired beside the petiole although sometime…
parole.testo: From French, from Latin stipula (“stalk (of hay), straw”).

parole.significato: Loud; shrill, piercing, high-pitched; rough-sounding.
parole.testo: From French strident, from Latin strīdēns, present active participle of strīdō.

parole.significato: Juicy or lush.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French succulent, from Latin succulentus.

parole.significato: A function for which every element of the codomain is mapped to by some element of the domain; (formally) Any function…

parole.significato: to surmise.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French surmetre, ultimately from Latin supermitto.

parole.significato: A translation of a segment of the libretto or other text or sometimes a brief summary of the plot projected onto a scre…
parole.testo: From French sur (“over, above”), from Latin super, + title, from Latin titulum.

parole.significato: A dominant nation or state that has control over the international affairs of a subservient state which otherwise has d…
parole.testo: From French suzerain, based on sus (“up, above”) (from Latin sursum) with the ending of souverain (whence also English sovereign).

parole.significato: A character or glyph representing an idea, concept or object.

parole.significato: Pertaining to a symbol.
parole.testo: From French symbolique or directly from Latin symbolicus, from Ancient Greek συμβολικός (sumbolikós, “of or belonging to a symbol”), equivalent to symbol + -ic.

parole.significato: The study of ancient symbols.
parole.testo: From French symbolique or Latin symbolicus, from Ancient Greek συμβολικός (sumbolikós, “of or belonging to a symbol”).

parole.significato: A type of red wine.

parole.significato: Tannin.

parole.significato: Tannic acid or any of its derivatives.
parole.testo: From French tannin, from Latin tannum (“oak bark”), from Gaulish *tannos (“oak”). Related to tan. By surface analysis, tann- + -in.

parole.significato: An insectivorous primate of the family Tarsiidae, having very large eyes and long feet, native mainly to several island…
parole.testo: From French tarsier, from Latin tarsus, from Ancient Greek ταρσός (tarsós, “wickerwork mat"; "broad, flat surface"”).

parole.significato: A dark brownish-grey colour, the colour of moleskin.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French taupe, from Latin talpa (“mole”). Doublet of talpa.

parole.significato: Pertaining to the Earth, earthly.
parole.testo: A borrowing of French tellurique, from Latin tellus (“earth; earthy”) and Tellus (“Earth, Gaia”) and -ique (forming adjectives). Subsequently also from tellurium, originally in telluric oxide from German Telluroxyd.

parole.significato: An outwork in the main ditch of a fortification, in front of the curtain, between two bastions.
parole.testo: From French tenaille (“a pair of pincers or tongs”), from its pincer-like shape, from Latin tenāculum. See tenaculum and tenaillon.

parole.significato: A cellular layer derived from the nucleus of an ovule and surrounding the embryo sac.

parole.significato: A single, distinctive rock formation; an area having a preponderance of a particular rock or group of rocks.

parole.significato: A steel pin in early rifles.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French tige (“stem”), from Latin tibia (“shin bone, leg”). Doublet of tibia.

parole.significato: A helmsman.

parole.significato: A decorative metalware having a lacquered or enamelled surface that is painted or gilded.

parole.significato: Fashion, the current style, the vogue.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French ton (“manner”), from Latin tonus. Doublet of tone, tune, and tonus.

parole.significato: A tightly braided necklace or collar, often made of metal, worn by various early European peoples.

parole.testo: Borrowed from French toxique, from Late Latin toxicus (“poisoned”), from Latin toxicum (“poison”), from Ancient Greek τοξικόν (toxikón) [φάρμακον (phármakon)] ("poison for use on arrows"), from τοξικός (toxikós, “pertaining to arrows or archery”), from τόξον (tóxon, “bow”).

parole.significato: The seasonal movement of grazing livestock (especially cattle, sheep, or goats) to new pastures which may be quite dist…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French transhumance, ultimately from Latin trāns (“across, beyond”) + humus (“ground”).

parole.significato: The act of passing over, across, or through something.

parole.significato: A trapezium.
parole.testo: From French trapèze, from Latin trapezium. Doublet of trapezium.

parole.significato: A resident of Three Rivers (Trois-Rivières) or its surrounding county.
parole.testo: From French trifluvien, equivalent to tri- + fluv- (from Latin fluvius (“river”)) + -ian. This is a latinate rendering of Three Rivers/Trois-Rivières, Quebec. Compare English fluvial.

parole.significato: One of the thickenings of the cell wall at the angles where several cells join.
parole.testo: From French trigone, from Latin trigōnum, from Ancient Greek τρῐ́γωνον (trĭ́gōnon). Doublet of trigon and trigonon.

parole.significato: A period of three months or about three months; (financial): quarter.
parole.testo: PIE word  *tréyes From French trimestre, from Latin trimestris (“of three months”), from trēs (“three”) + mensis (“month”).

parole.significato: A metrical foot in verse consisting of a stressed or heavy syllable followed by an unstressed or light syllable.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French trochée, via Latin trochaeus from the Ancient Greek τροχαῖος (trokhaîos), derived from τρέχω (trékhō, “run”).

parole.significato: The state of being truculent; eagerness to fight; ferocity.
parole.testo: From French truculence, from Latin truculentia.

parole.significato: A kind of silk lace or light netting, used for clothing, veils, etc.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French tulle, named after French Tulle (a town), named after Latin Tūtēla (a Roman deity), from Latin tūtēla (whence English tutelary), from Latin tueor (whence tutor, tutorial).

parole.significato: To cause to swell.

parole.significato: A whirlwind or vortex.

parole.testo: Borrowed from French turbine, from Latin turbō, turbinem (“tornado, whirlwind; crowd”).

parole.significato: A powdered form of impure zinc oxide used for polishing.
parole.testo: From French tutie; compare Spanish tutía, atutía, from Latin tutia, from Arabic تُوتِيَاء (tūtiyāʔ), from Classical Persian توتیا (tūtyā), from Sanskrit तुत्था (tutthā).

parole.significato: The killing of a tyrant.
parole.testo: From French tyrannicide, from Middle French tyrannicide, from Latin tyrannicīda. Equivalent to tyrant + -cide.

parole.significato: Someone who kills a tyrant.
parole.testo: From French tyrannicide, from Middle French tyrannicide, from Latin tyrannicīdium. Equivalent to tyrant + -cide.

parole.significato: Ultimate; final.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French ultime.

parole.significato: Being the only one of its kind; unequaled, unparalleled or unmatched.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French unique, from Latin unicus.

parole.significato: The diachronic process of forming a new single word from a fixed expression of several words.
parole.testo: Probably from French univerbation, from uni- (“uni-”) + Latin verbum (“word”) + French -ation (“-ation”).

parole.significato: To commit usury.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French usure (“usury”, noun). The change to a verb in English may be influenced by back-formation from usury. Piecewise doublet of etymology 2.

parole.significato: One who murders one's wife.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French uxoricide or Latin uxor + English -icide.

parole.significato: The murdering of one's own wife.
parole.testo: From French uxoricide or Latin uxōricīdium.

parole.significato: evaporation
parole.testo: Compare French vaporation, Latin vaporatio.

parole.significato: An imperfection on the inside of the hind leg in horses, different from a curb, but at the same height, and often growi…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French varisse, from Latin varis-, oblique stem of varis. Compare varix and French varice.

parole.significato: A conveyance: a spacious device for carrying or transporting substances, objects, people or animals.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French véhicule, from Latin vehiculum (“a carriage, conveyance”), from vehō, vehere (“to carry”).

parole.significato: An early two-wheeled conveyance upon which one rode astride a wooden frame propelled by means of pushing the feet again…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French vélocipède, from Latin velox (“swift”) + pes (“foot”).

parole.significato: For sale; available for purchase.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French vénal, from Old French venel, from Latin vēnālis (“for sale”), from vēnum (“something for sale”); compare English vend.

parole.significato: The fact or state of being for sale, especially with reference to bribes or corruption.
parole.testo: From venal + -ity, from French vénalité or Latin vēnālitās, from vēnālis (“venal”), from vēnum; compare English vend.

parole.significato: Synonym of sell, (now especially) to sell through a vending machine.
parole.testo: 17th century, likely a backformation from earlier vendible, vendee, vendor inspired by the underlying French vendre, from Old French vendre, from Latin vendere, from vēnum dāre (“to give (something for) sale”).

parole.significato: Synonym of venom.
parole.testo: From French venin (“venom”), from Latin venēnum (“juice; venom”). Doublet of venene and venom.

parole.significato: To sell; to vend.

parole.significato: A pebble or little stone shaped and polished by wind-blown sand.

parole.significato: Related to the abdomen or stomach.
parole.testo: From French ventral, from Latin ventrālis, from venter (“belly, abdomen”); by surface analysis, ventr- + -al.

parole.significato: Experienced, practiced.

parole.significato: A joint of the back.
parole.testo: From French vertebre, from Latin vertebra.

parole.significato: A sleeveless garment that buttons down the front, worn over a shirt, and often as part of a suit; a waistcoat.
parole.testo: Derived from French veste (“a vest, jacket”), from Latin vestis (“a garment, gown, robe, vestment, clothing, vesture”), from Proto-Indo-European *wéstis, from *wes- (“to be dressed”) (English wear). Cognate with Sanskrit वस्त्र (vastra) and Spanish vestir.

parole.significato: To furnish with a vestibule or vestibules.
parole.testo: Early 17th century, borrowed from French vestibule (“entrance court”), from Latin vestibulum (“forecourt, entrance court; entrance”), from vestiō (“to dress, clothe, vest”) + -bulum (“place, location”, nominal suffix). Doublet of vestibulum.

parole.significato: A mark left on the earth by a foot.
parole.testo: From French vestige, from Latin vestīgium (“footstep, footprint, track, the sole of the foot, a trace, mark”). Doublet of vestigium.

parole.significato: Pulsing with energy or activity.
parole.testo: From French vibrant, from Latin vibrans, present participle of vibrare (“to vibrate”). See vibrate.

parole.significato: The act of vibrating or the condition of being vibrated.
parole.testo: From French vibration, from Latin vibrātiō (“a shaking or brandishing”), from vibrō (“shake, vibrate”); see vibrate. Morphologically vibrate + -ion.

parole.significato: Watchful, especially for danger or disorder; alert; wary.
parole.testo: From French vigilant or its source, Latin vigilans, present participle of vigilare (“stay awake”), from vigil (“awake”). Doublet of vigilante, from Spanish. Displaced Old English wacor.

parole.significato: A running ornament consisting of leaves and tendrils, used in Gothic architecture.
parole.testo: First attested in 1751. From French vignette, diminutive of vigne (“vine”), from Latin vīnea, from vīnum (“wine”). Replaced earlier Middle English vynet.

parole.significato: The waste liquor remaining in the process of making beet sugar, used in the manufacture of fertiliser or potassium carb…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French vinasse, ultimately from Latin vīnācea.

parole.significato: Synonym of slash ⟨/⟩.
parole.testo: An anglicization of French virgule, from Latin virgula.

parole.significato: A permit to enter and leave a country, normally issued by the authorities of the country to be visited.
parole.testo: From 1831, "official signature or endorsement on a passport," from French visa, from Latin charta vīsa (“paper that has been seen”) from feminine perfect passive of Latin vidēre (“to see”). Compare vision, video, vista.

parole.significato: A curtain of light translucent material intended to be secured directly to the woodwork of a French window or glazed do…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French vitrage (literally “glass covering”), ultimately from Latin vitrum (“glass”).

parole.significato: A glass-paneled cabinet or case, especially for displaying articles such as china, objets d'art, fine merchandise, natu…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French vitrine, from vitre (“pane of glass”), from Old French, from Latin vitrum (“glass”).

parole.significato: A carriage; a vehicle, now chiefly in French contexts.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French voiture, from Latin vectūra. Doublet of vecture and vettura.

parole.significato: The staff of an army, including all officers above the rank of colonel, all adjutants, inspectors, quartermasters, comm…
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French, from état (“state”) + Latin major (“greater”).
